Posts 3 By Matt Goldberg Apr 29, 2010 However, the true star of Empire is undoubtedly Henson as Cookie, which won Henson a Golden Globe for "Best Performance by an Actress In A Television Series." Henson plays the character as witty yet also intensely petty and sometimes cruel, with one-liners such as summing up Hakeem\'s entire character with "You need to stop rappin\' like you from the streets, \'cause you not about that life!" or shutting down Lucious\' advances on her by saying "Get rid of fake-ass Halle Berry. As long as she\'s around, I\'m closed for business." With these lines, Henson doesn\'t just make the audience laugh with her sassy and snappy delivery, but plays a similar role to Cersei ( Lena Headey ) in later seasons of Game of Thrones , where there is something delightful about watching a woman outdo the men around her in a male-dominated world. She can even be unnecessarily blunt, telling Jamal that, "For a queen, you sure do keep a messy place. What you need is a good maid up in here." While a borderline homophobic thing to say, the context of Cookie\'s persona and love for her children keeps her sympathetic rather than making us hate her. \'Empire\' Changed How Music Was Viewed in TV Hakeem, Jamal, Cookie, and Lucious singing in the studio in Empire Image via FOX Being a show about musicians trying to take over a record label, Empire comes with some absolute bangers that are original songs from the actors that went far beyond the show\'s fanbase. In 2015, the Season 1 soundtrack hit #1 on the Billboard charts , the first to do so since Glee , which featured cover music . Incorporating this into the show, from boardrooms to recording booths, meant there was a versatility to Empire’s success and tone not often seen on today’s television. Some shows do attempt to replicate it, such as how The Witcher saw success with Joey Batey \'s recordings of songs like "Toss a Coin to Your Witcher," and "Burn Butcher Burn," which have over 100 million and 46 million streams on Spotify, respectively. But Empire paved the way for this kind of creative experimentation. While some may consider Empire to be a guilty pleasure, considering the dramatized nature of the characters and world they exist within, which sets it apart from the more grounded and nuanced world of Succession , there is no reason why you shouldn\'t embrace said pleasure. Cookie certainly wouldn\'t blame you. With some standout performances and trailblazing history, Empire isn\'t like many 5-season shows you\'ll watch, and that makes it all the juicier for your binge satisfaction. Videos 2025 Movie Releases Screenings What to Watch Originals Reviews Close 10 Epic Movies That Are Incredible From Start to Finish Neytiri and Jake looking at white floaty things in Avatar (2009) Image via 20th Century Studios By Jiminna Shillingford Published Nov 14, 2025 Jiminna Shillingford is an avid reader and a passionate storyteller. She is obsessed with all things TV, from anime and romantic fantasy to action-packed series. With that deep affection, Jiminna longs to share her excitement with all her readers through the Collider platform as a TV author. Through her writing she has created stories and blog posts of amazing book recommendations, showcasing her love of writing. Jiminna's goal is to inspire others to discover and embrace their love of stories in all of its forms. Sign in to your Collider account Summary Generate a summary of this story follow Follow followed Followed Like Like Thread Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap Epic films have an incredible ability: they hook viewers into their realm of brilliance within the very first few minutes, and don't let go until the screen goes dark . Whether it's universe-shifting stakes or quality character arcs, quite a few movies have earned the status of being the greatest from start to finish, delivering cinematic journeys that are remembered long after the credits roll. A few epic triumphs are films like Gladiator , which immerses its viewers in the rich ancient world of Rome, and Spider-Man: No Way Home , which reshapes a hero’s journey in unexpected ways. They may be two vastly different cinematic experiences, but both stand as quality epic films. On this list are some of the most epic movies to hit the screens—experiences crafted for viewers' pleasure that genuinely grip them from beginning to end . 10 'Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon' (2000) Yu Shu Lien brandishes her jian sword Image via Sony Pictures Classics Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon is a wuxia gem that introduced the genre to a global mainstream audience. The 2000s fantasy film follows renowned swordsman Li Mu Bai ( Chow Yun-Fat ), who has made the decision to retire and entrusts his legendary sword, the Green Destiny, to his friend . In a twist of fate, the sword is stolen by the willful aristocratic daughter of a governor, Jen ( Zhang Ziyi ), who has been secretly honing her martial skills. Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon is a universally acclaimed masterpiece that not only earned itself 40 awards worldwide but is also praised for some of the best action sequences seen to date. The martial arts scenes are visually pleasing as they unfold like epic, dance-like sequences of graceful yet intense violent combat all throughout its run. From the film's gorgeous cinematography of China’s landscapes to its intimate story of duty, love, and freedom, Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon is an epic movie that remains one of the most beautiful and influential watches from beginning to end. 9 'Spirited Away' (2001) Chihiro standing among flowers and looking up in 'Spirited Away'. Image via Studio Ghibli This enticing fantasy film is often hailed as one of the greatest animated movies of all time . Spirited Away centers around 10-year-old Chihiro ( Rumi Hiiragi ), who winds up in a mysterious spirit realm and is forced into servitude by a cunning witch named Yubaba ( Mari Natsuki ), in order to survive and free her parents, who have been transformed into pigs. The anime epic took both children and adults on a journey of pure imagination and wonder. Its impact pushed the world to pay far more attention to the anime genre, as the movie stunned audiences so thoroughly with its universal themes of courage and friendship, and incredibly beautiful hand-drawn animation. Throughout the entire film, Spirited Away catapults its viewers into an extremely immersive and transformative adventure that feels much larger than its actual runtime, making it the ideal pick for this list of epic films. 8 'Titanic' (1997) Kate Winslet as Rose looks over Leonardo DiCaprio's shoulder at a drawing in Titanic. Image via 20th Century Studios Titanic is as epic as they come, standing as a highly beloved and devotedly cherished romance film . The movie, set in 1912, follows 17-year-old Rose DeWitt Bukater ( Kate Winslet ) as she boards the RMS Titanic as a first-class passenger with her stunningly wealthy family and boastful fiancé. Suffocating and suffering in a loveless relationship, Rose's contemplation of suicide halts as she encounters the dashing third-class passenger Jack Dawson ( Leonardo DiCaprio ). Titanic is a timeless gem of love and wonder that spans three incredible hours and is worth every minute of it. It stands now as more than a blockbuster hit—it's an undeniable cinematic phenomenon that wields a sweeping romance for the ages. Not one moment of the film is dull or falters in quality; for audiences, every minute is spent in Titanic's hypnotic blend of personal romance and historical tragedy. Titanic is an emotional journey that’s capable of thoroughly sweeping its audiences away from start to finish—a reminder that even love can outlive death. 7 'Gladiator' (2000) Russell Crowe looking upset in a tunic in Gladiator Image via Universal Pictures This Roman epic is a true tale of “sword-and-sandal.” The film Gladiator is set in 180 AD and centers around the respected general, Maximus Decimus Meridius ( Russell Crowe ), who, after a petty betrayal at the hands of the ambitious and cruel Commodus ( Joaquin Phoenix ) , is forced into slavery as a gladiator. Gladiator is an Oscar-worthy drama that delivers a crowd-pleasing spectacle in the best way. From its opening battles to its opulent arenas of Rome, Gladiator brought to life an epic and ancient world during its premiere, captivating its audience in a world of unmatched intensity for its entire runtime. Gladiator still remains an epic watch rife with rich storytelling, lavish production, and a larger-than-life atmosphere—a true modern historical classic that is the epitome of the epic movie experience. 6 'Spider-Man: Across The Spider-Verse' (2023) Miguel pins down Miles as he tries to escape the Spiderverse in Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse. Image via Sony Pictures Releasing Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse is the second movie in the Miles Morales ( Shameik Moore ), Spider-Man films . The incredibly epic animated movie continues Miles' journey as a more mature superhero, who unexpectedly encounters a seemingly low-level villain called The Spot ( Jason Schwartzman )—only for that encounter to spiral into a multiversal crisis that threatens multiple universes and Miles’ happiness. After the hit movie Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse , quite a few fans believed that the story couldn’t get any better-and boy, were they mistaken . Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse not only delivers brilliant animated battles but also an unexpected emotional depth that elevates the film’s story by leaps and bounds. Audiences have frequently sung the movie’s praises, lauding it as one of the most dazzlingly bold and emotionally rich watches made in some time. With high, immersive stakes, creative multiverse storytelling, and a soundtrack worth talking about , Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse gifts audiences an incredible cinematic journey—one that has been consistently hailed as the greatest animated film of the decade, and is worth every minute of its runtime. 5 'Zack Snyder's Justice League' (2021) zack-snyders-justice-league-david-thewlis-ares-darkseid Image via HBO Max This iconic director’s cut is one of the best things to make it out of the 2021 cinematic universe . Zack Snyder’s Justice League delivers the complete four-hour vision that expands the film’s 2017 theatrical cut, following the death of the beloved hero Superman ( Henry Cavill ). With Earth truly vulnerable, the ancient evil, Steppenwolf ( Ciarán Hinds ), arrives to recover three Mother Boxes, with intentions of conquering Earth for the malicious, power-seeker monster, Darkseid ( Ray Porter ). The Snyder Cut is one of the biggest film turnarounds seen in cinematic history. The film, four hours long, has been lauded as one of the most unexpectedly entertaining superhero watches to make it onto screens—enhancing what was once only a potentially fantastic story through its extended reveals. From the movie’s rich operatic tone and mythic cinematography to the film’s epic fight sequences, Zack Snyder’s Justice League is a monumental and unforgettable experience from start to finish. 4 'Avatar' (2009) Neytiri and Jake in a Pandora forest in Avatar 2009 Image via 20th Century Studios Avatar is a true storm of epic proportions in the cinematic universe . The worldwide phenomenon is set in the mid-22nd century and centers around paralyzed former Marine, Jake Sully ( Sam Worthington ), who, due to his brother’s untimely death, is recruited to operate an “avatar”—a genetically engineered Na’vi-human hybrid—on the alien moon Pandora. From its incredible 3D technology to its emotional storytelling, Avatar stands as a timeless cinematic masterpiece for the ages. The film’s world-building is incredibly astonishing, while its action scenes are just as breathtaking —delivering absolute cinematic excellence for its entire runtime . With soaring scores and visuals quite literally able to stun its viewers, Avatar offers a perfect and extremely influential work of art that never falters in its high quality, from its opening scenes to its rolling credits. To date, the movie remains one of the highest-grossing films of all time, making it the ideal pick for this list of epic movies. 3 'Spider-Man: No Way Home' (2021) Tom Holland in his Spider-Man uniform with the mask off in Spider-Man: No Way Home. Image via Sony Pictures Releasing This movie masterpiece is one that artfully celebrates the treasured legacy of Spider-Man . Spider-Man: No Way Home follows the repercussions of Peter Parker's ( Tom Holland ) shocking unmasking. In a bid to return his life to the way it was, Peter seeks help from the time-altering Doctor Strange ( Benedict Cumberbatch ), only for things to go incredibly wrong, with the opening of the multiverse. No Way Home is the perfect homage to a strong legacy that has entertained millions for decades. The film skillfully blends fan service, nostalgia, and emotional storytelling—offering audiences a thrill ride from beginning to end . This epic superhero installment is one for the books, ultimately revealing that the entire trilogy is one long origin story for Holland’s Spider-Man. With a host of incredible action, iconic multiverse crossovers, and a story detailing the culmination of self-sacrifice, Spider-Man: No Way Home is an unforgettably epic experience that landed itself in the superhero film hall of fame. 2 'Avengers: Endgame' (2019) Robert Downey Jr. as Tony Stark / Iron Man snapping to end the battle in Avengers:Endgame Image via Marvel Studios Avengers: Endgame is a standing masterpiece of the superhero genre . The film, a culmination of the Marvel Cinematic Universe’s first grand saga, picks up five years after the heartbreaking events of Infinity War . Avengers: Endgame is the perfect ending to a saga of pure epicness. The movie’s three-hour runtime is filled with rich storytelling and unbelievable action from start to finish . The film shook the world as it became a true global cinematic event of an unprecedented scale, immediately after its premiere—highly praised for its narrative ambition rife with character and heart. With stunning battle sequences, a thrilling story, and brilliant production, Avengers: Endgame gifts audiences an emotionally satisfying climax that offers closure on beloved characters and years of amazing storytelling. 1 'The Dark Knight' (2008) Batman racing through the streets in The Dark Knight (2008) Image via Warner Bros. Pictures This genre-defining superhero epic is widely hailed as not only one of the best superhero films ever made, but one of the absolute best thrill rides from beginning to end . The Dark Knight follows the beloved vigilante of Gotham City, Bruce Wayne/Batman ( Christian Bale ), as he faces his greatest challenge yet—criminal mastermind, Joker ( Heath Ledger ). The Dark Knight transcended the superhero genre during its premiere and is now frequently regarded as a modern epic crime thriller that features some of the most treasured comic book characters. Heath Ledger’s performance alone can be considered one of the greatest portrayals seen in cinematic history—elevating an already standout film. From its consistent tension during its two-and-a-half-hour run to its iconic, award-winning performances, The Dark Knight stands as a groundbreaking masterpiece that features some of the most epic storytelling seen on the big screen. I Bet These 10 Movies Can (and Will) Change Your Mind The villainous Lord Farquaad smiles to himself in Shrek . Image via DreamWorks Animation By Tyler B. Searle Published 5 days ago Born with Autism (formerly classified as Asperger syndrome), Tyler B. Searle has been obsessed with storytelling since he was old enough to speak. He gravitated towards fairy tales, mythology, the fantasy genre, and animated movies and shows aimed at family audiences. When not writing, Tyler enjoys watching more cartoons and reading fantasy books in his home in Ontario, Canada. Sign in to your Collider account follow Follow followed Followed Like Like Thread 1 Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap Fantasy is perhaps the most diverse and creative genre of storytelling because it allows us to make sense of the world around us and our emotions through symbolism and metaphors in the shape of everything from talking animals, valiant knights, fire-breathing dragons, and lands where magic and mystery abound. Fantasy allows us to confront the problems in our everyday lives by showing how they can be overcome in an out-of-this-world setting. Fantasy is also a very malleable genre; any story can be considered a fantasy if it has mystical and supernatural elements. Thus, it can also be paired with other genres, which can help encourage people who might normally overlook fantasy stories to give it a chance. Granted, there\'s nothing wrong with disliking a genre for one reason or another, but this aversion might be due to a lack of understanding of what fantasy actually is. This list includes several movies that best represent the genre , both high and low, both sweet and sorrowful. They encompass the genre\'s strongest elements and can make a believer out of those who dislike fantasy the most . \'Stardust\' (2007) Claire Danes and Charlie Cox looking stunned in a scene from Stardust. Image via Paramount Pictures Tristan Thron ( Charlie Cox ) is a young man living in the village of Wall on the edge of the magic kingdom of Stormhold, who longs to win the affection of a woman named Victoria ( Sienna Miller ). One night, they witness a star falling from the sky, and Tristan vows to retrieve it for her in exchange for her hand in marriage. However, the star has taken the form of a human woman named Yvaine ( Claire Danes ), and others are eager to claim her as well, such as a trio of witches who want to use her heart to regain their youth, and the princes of Stormhold, who want the ruby that knocked Yvaine from the sky in the first place. Stardust has quite a few differences from Neil Gaiman \'s novel that help make it a more casual and enjoyable movie. It does down a lot of the darker parts for a more lighthearted rom-com tone , allowing for quirky characters and a very cute romance between Thrstan and Yvaine. The acting also helps add to the charm, with Michelle Pfeiffer giving an enjoyable, wicked performance as the lead witch, Mark Strong beginning his villain career with the evil Prince Septimus, and Robert De Niro stealing the show as the crossdressing and cultured sky pirate, Captain Shakespeare. \'The Dark Crystal\' (1982) A sill image from the 1982 dark fantasy film, The Dark Crystal. Image via Universal Pictures Jen ( Stephen Garlick ) is one of the last Gelflings left on the planet Thra, and lives with the wise urRu, mystical ancients who hide from the tyrannical and decadent Skeksis who rule Thra. When their Master ( Brian Muehl ) dies, he tells Jen to seek out the wise woman Aughra ( Billie Whitelaw ) and retrieve a shard of the Dark Crystal that the Skeksis use to control Thra and extend their lives. If Jen can repair the crystal before the Great Conjunction of the world\'s three suns, he can save Thra and bring an end to Skeksis rule. Few movies reach the same level of immersion as The Dark Crystal . Thanks to masterful puppetry and a lack of human characters, the movie truly feels like you\'ve stepped into a world completely foreign to ours, where nearly everything is alive and active with unique movements. The Skeksis are the standout creatures in the film: they are highly expressive thanks to articulate facial features and flamboyant personalities, making them the perfect allegory for avarice, tyranny, and decadence. \'The Shape of Water\' (2017) Sally Hawkins as Elisa and Doug Jones as The Amphibian Man lock eyes through a tank in The Shape of Water. Image via Searchlight Pictures Elisa Esposito ( Sally Hawkins ) is a mute woman working at a secret government laboratory during the Cold War, whose only friends include her coworker Zelda ( Octavia Spencer ) and her neighbor, Giles ( Richard Jenkins ). One day, Colonel Richard Strickland ( Michael Shannon ) arrives at the lab with a revolutionary discovery: an amphibious humanoid ( Doug Jones ). As Strickland instructs his scientists to study the creature\'s respiratory system, Elisa enlists her friends to help free him, and she and the creature develop a romantic connection. The Shape of Water is Guillermo del Toro \'s hybridization of Creature from the Black Lagoon and Beauty and the Beast , resulting in one of the most unique romance stories in cinema . Its success comes from how the film deconstructs the idea of "the other" and society\'s habit of demonizing those who do not fit in with the accepted norm. Thus, the love that blooms between Elisa and the creature demonstrates the power of human empathy as those considered "others" can find solace in one another. \'Everything Everywhere All at Once\' (2022) Image via A24 Evelyn Quan Wang ( Michelle Yeoh ) is a struggling Chinese American who is juggling the IRS and an estranged relationship with her husband Waymond ( Ke Huy Quan ) and daughter Joy ( Stephanie Hsu ). One day, Evelyn learns about the multiverse, which is under threat of destruction due to the mysterious Jobu Tupaki. Evelyn gains the ability to hop into alternate versions of herself and access their memories and skills, which she uses to try and stop Jobu while trying to find fulfillment in her life choices. Everything Everywhere All at Once is a visually stunning movie that takes the audience on an absurdist multiversal journey that touches on powerful existential themes . Nihilism is a major theme here, using the multiverse and the concept of infinite choices to question whether anything in existence matters, and if so, what gives life meaning? The actors do a phenomenal job bringing their characters to life, particularly Yeoh, whose balance of comedic timing and emotional pathos anchors the film\'s emotional core. \'The Secret of Kells\' (2009) Brendan writing in a book with a quill while Aidan looks on in The Secret of Kells. Image via Buena Vista International Brendan ( Evan McGuire ) is a young boy living with his uncle, Cellach ( Brendan Gleeson ), the abbot of Kells, who is focused on building a wall to protect the abbey from invading Northmen. One day, they are visited by Brother Aidan ( Mick Lally ), a master illuminator who has come from the island of Iona with an unfinished manuscript. Since his age is impacting his ability to illuminate the book, Aidan recruits Brendan to help him, and Brendan also befriends a mysterious girl from the forest named Aisling ( Christen Mooney ). The Secret of Kells can best be summed up in one word: magical . Its stylistic animation and vibrant colors do a phenomenal job mimicking the style of a medieval illuminated manuscript come to life, and help to give the film a mystical quality that highlights the more fantastical elements of the story, especially Aisling. It\'s also not afraid to show off some dark imagery, especially when the Viking soldiers arrive, which helps remind us to enjoy the moments of beauty while they last. \'The Princess Bride\' (1987) Westley stands on guard with his sword while Buttercup stands behind him in The Princess Bride. Image via 20th Century Studios A grandfather ( Peter Falk ) reads a bedtime story to his sick grandson ( Fred Savage ). It follows a peasant woman named Buttercup ( Robin Wright ), who loses her love, Westley ( Cary Elwes ), while he is at sea, and is chosen by Prince Humperdinck ( Chris Sarandon ) to be his bride. However, Buttercup is abducted by a trio of bandits who hope to start a war with Humperdinck\'s enemies, but their attempts to flee with her are thwarted by a mysterious and highly skilled man in black. The Princess Bride was a commercial failure on release, but has since developed a large cult following that has elevated it to one of the best fantasy films ever made . It knows exactly what it is: a low-stakes film that embraces classic tropes and is full of heartfelt romance, exciting swordfights, and quirky dialogue . The cast is also a big reason for the film\'s likability, thanks to their great repertoire and ability to immerse themselves in the role, especially Mandy Patinkin as the Spanish fencer Inigo Montoya. \'Shrek\' (2001) Shrek in the first Shrek movie. Image via DreamWorks Animation When Lord Farquaad ( John Lithgow ) of Duloc banishes all fairy tale creatures from his land, they are forced into a swamp owned by an antisocial ogre named Shrek ( Mike Myers ). When Shrek confronts him about this, Farquaad agrees to remove the squatters if Shrek goes to a dragon-guarded castle to rescue his intended bride, Princess Fiona ( Cameron Diaz ). With the aid of a talking donkey ( Eddie Murphy ), Shrek agrees to the task, but discovers that there is a lot more to this princess than first appears. Shrek changed the world of animated films on release, and also ushered in a new era of fairy tale satire with its cynical jokes and less-than-appealing visuals. Over 20 years later, the film remains iconic thanks to the emotional weight behind its characters and story. When you get past the hilarious jokes and the jabs at Disney, Shrek is a movie about finding acceptance from yourself and others, as well as a reminder not to judge others before you get to know them. \'Pan\'s Labyrinth\' (2006) Image via Warner Bros. Pictures Ofelia ( Ivana Baquero ) is a young girl living in Francoist Spain, whose pregnant mother has recently married Captain Vidal ( Sergi López ), a staunch Falangist. One night, she follows a fairy into a subterranean labyrinth and meets a faun ( Doug Jones ), who tells her that she is the reincarnation of the princess of the underworld. To re-enter her kingdom, she must complete three dangerous tasks, all while still tending to her ill mother and avoiding Vidal\'s wrath as he ruthlessly hunts down Maquis rebels. Pan\'s Labyrinth is a masterpiece of dark fantasy that weaves its fantastical elements into the day-to-day struggles that Ofelia goes through in such a tumultuous period. The most obvious example is the Pale Man (Doug Jones), a decrepit creature that sits before a lavish feast. Rather than eat it himself, he uses it to lure children for him to devour, much like how vile regimes destroy their youth in the name of ideology. It also delves into dark themes of resistance and self-sacrifice , which lead to a beautifully bittersweet ending open to interpretation. \'The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring\' (2001) In the pleasant green land of the Shire, the hobbit Bilbo Baggins ( Sir Ian Holm ) vanishes during his 111th birthday party, and leaves all of his possessions to his nephew, Frodo ( Elijah Wood ). Among his inheritance is a magic gold ring that, unfortunately, is identified as the One Ring forged by the Dark Lord Sauron ( Alan Howard ), and within which is contained a great portion of his power and will to dominate. On the advice of the wizard Gandalf ( Sir Ian McKellen ), Frodo and three companions—his friend Samwise Gamgee ( Sean Aston ), and his cousins Meriadoc Brandybuck ( Dominic Monnaham ) and Peregrin Took ( Billy Boyd )—make for the elven city of Rivendell to seek council from Lord Elrond ( Hugo Weaving ), but the servants of Sauron are close at hand. The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring marks the beginning of Sir Peter Jackson \'s legendary film trilogy , which proved that fantasy movies had the punch to be epic blockbusters . It\'s all thanks to how masterfully it weaves together multiple film techniques and special effects, including specially designed sets to make the Hobbit characters look smaller than everyone else, gorgeous landscapes and map paintings that successfully transport the audience into a fantasy world , and great practical effects, costumes, and CGI to make the creatures feel alive. But it\'s the emotions of the story that truly hook you: the actors perfectly embody each of their characters, and as such, the weight of the mission and their individual friendships are felt fully. \'Spirited Away\' (2001) Chihiro holding into Haku as he flies above the river in Spirited Away Image via Studio Ghibli On the way to their new home, Chihiro ( Rumi Hiiragi/Daveigh Chase ) and her parents stumble into the spirit world and become trapped at sundown. Her parents are turned into pigs, but Chihiro is saved by a boy named Haku ( Miyu Irino/Jason Marsden ), who helps her get a job at the local bathhouse run by the witch Yubaba ( Mari Natsuki/Suzanne Pleshette ). If Chihiro wants to save her parents and get back home, she\'ll have to make friends with spirits who have a low view of humans and make sense of the world\'s strange laws and customs. It might have taken 20 years for New Zealand director Peter Jackson\'s plucky fantasy to clamber, Mount-Doom-style, to the very pinnacle of our greatest-movies pantheon. But here it is, brighter and more resplendent than ever. The Fellowship Of The Ring contains so much movie. Even at the halfway point, as the characters take a breather to bicker in Rivendell, you already feel sated, like you\'ve experienced more thrills, more suspense, more jollity and ethereal beauty than a regular film could possibly muster up. Kenji Fujishima | Off-Broadway | November 17, 2025 Wai Ching Ho, Cindy Cheung, Jon Norman Schneider, and Amy Keum star in Alex Lin’s Laowang: A Chinatown King Lear , directed by Joshua Kahan Brody for Primary Stages at 59E59 Theaters. (© James Leynse) The inspiration for Laowang couldn’t be clearer, since it’s subtitled A Chinatown King Lear , with “laowang” Chinese for “old king.” Some of the fun of this new play lies in seeing the ways playwright Alex Lin has transposed the characters and plot points of William Shakespeare’s classic tragedy to New York City. But thankfully, Lin’s play, making its world premiere via Primary Stages, has enough of a distinctive profile to stand on its own. Margaret Choy (Wai Ching Ho)—referred to throughout the play as A-Poh, the Chinese term for maternal grandmother—is Laowang ‘s Lear equivalent. She’s the owner of China Bull & Bear, a long-running restaurant in Chinatown that has been closed for a few months at the start of the play. Real-estate developer Wesley Chiu (Daisuke Tsuji), who worked as a dishwasher there as a kid, is angling to buy the building and redevelop it into condos and a museum commemorating the restaurant. The ever-prideful A-Poh plays hardball with him in negotiations, suggesting a counteroffer far above Wesley’s initial pitch. Even before the deal has been finalized, two of A-Poh’s three grandchildren see dollar signs in their eyes. Both Amy (Cindy Cheung) and Steven (Jon Norman Schneider) have long since moved away from New York, with only Lai-Fa (Amy Keum) still living near A-Poh. The heated exchanges all three of them have with each other throughout suggest a host of familial resentments. To Amy and Steven, Lai-Fa was clearly A-Poh’s favorite, since she was spared the ill treatment they received from her when they both worked at China Bull & Bear as children. Thus, they are especially driven to snatch power of attorney over the restaurant for themselves while Lai-Fa desires to keep the establishment. Wesley, additionally motivated by personal reasons revealed later in the play, manipulates these tensions for his own gain. Amy Keum plays Lai-Fa in Alex Lin’s Laowang: A Chinatown King Lear , directed by Joshua Kahan Brody for Primary Stages at 59E59 Theaters. (© James Leynse) If we consider these characters in the shadow of King Lear , Amy and Steven are the conniving Goneril and Reagan to Lai-Fa’s devoted Cordelia, with Wesley roughly standing in as its Edmund equivalent. And as with Lear, A-Poh is stricken with a madness of her own, diagnosed here as dementia. However, A-Poh’s mental decline is used as a pretext to offer glimpses into her past: the beginnings of her life in New York as an immigrant from Hong Kong; the scrappy genesis of her restaurant, and the ruthlessness with which she ran her business, including firing her head chef and replacing her with young Steven. (Cheung, Schneider, Keum, and Tsuji all double as an array of additional characters, with Cheung playing a younger version of Margaret and Schneider playing her late husband Jeffrey.) It’s in these flashbacks that the cultural specificity of Lin’s riff on Shakespeare shines through most brightly. Through them, we see glimpses of an immigrant who felt a need to risk forsaking her Asian identity, including adapting Chinese cuisine in her restaurant for American palates, to survive amid the dominant white culture. That hardly excuses the shortcuts she took, including using free child labor, to maximize profits. As objectionable as some of the behavior is, though, Lin always takes care to make their motivations understandable. She also brings refreshing glints of raucous humor to the proceedings; some of Wesley’s methods of manipulating both Amy and Steven are memorably, hilariously bawdy in nature. Wai Ching Ho plays A-Poh in Alex Lin’s Laowang: A Chinatown King Lear , directed by Joshua Kahan Brody for Primary Stages at 59E59 Theaters. (© James Leynse) Sharp performances help bring out the standout personal qualities in Lin’s writing. As the resentful Amy and Steven, Cheung and Schneider attack some of Lin’s funnier lines with screwball gusto, while Keum radiates innocence and concern as the devoted Lai-Fa. Tsuji smartly downplays Wesley’s villainy, thereby allowing the play’s inner concern with the perils of gentrification to come through lightly yet unmistakably. And Ho brings a balance of warmth and arrogance to A-Poh that makes the character magnetic even at her most imperious. Joshua Kahan Brody’s direction keeps the play’s mix of comic and tragic tones nicely in fulcrum. Wilson Chin’s scenic design cleverly uses curtains to indicate A-Poh’s dementia-induced flashback episodes, as does Reza Behjat’s lighting design. Costume designer Tina McCartney makes sure to clothe the characters in outfits appropriate to their personalities and cultural identities. Sound designer/composer Nicholas Drashner uses whispers at one point to hauntingly evoke A-Poh’s addled mental state. Laowang is the first of two plays by Alex Lin this season, the second being Roundabout Theatre Company’s upcoming production of Chinese Republicans . This affecting King Lear variation suggests she has a genuinely fresh perspective—warm and wise but also tough-minded and wickedly funny—to bring to depictions of the Asian-American experience in theater. Ranking them is a subjective affair, of course, and for many of the Netflix characters, a lower rank isn\'t about the actor, but rather the hand they were dealt. Let\'s take a look back at our favorite heroes — and a few villains, too. 15. Danny Rand, Iron Fist Netflix We said what we said, but it\'s difficult to defend Netflix\'s take on Danny Rand. Iron Fist creator Roy Thomas gives it a good shot , however. Finn Jones spends his two seasons limping through terrible fight choreography and a script that doesn\'t fit, well, much of anything. Visually, he\'s a good Iron Fist, and the contrast of his uptown life with Matt Murdock\'s grimier existence in the Hell\'s Kitchen neighborhood is nifty. But the glimpses of K\'un-Lun were whelming at release, and the lush fantasy of "Shang-Chi" makes this secretive Chinese realm now look like the back seat of a \'98 Camry. The best part of Rand\'s existence is watching him get sandbagged by every other character throughout "The Defenders." On the bright side, there\'s a way to redeem "Iron Fist" in our hearts. Read "The Immortal Iron Fist" by Ed Brubaker and Matt Fraction, currently available in an omnibus collection, and, if you like, follow along as Marvel Comics prepares to reboot the character with a new identity this year. 14. Cornell Beltram Stokes, Cottonmouth Netflix "Luke Cage" started off strong out the gate with the return of its titular character to his Harlem home. As he reasserts himself on the city streets, he quickly runs afoul of Cornell Stokes\' criminal family. Cottonmouth isn\'t a fan of his nickname, but he does understand the cruel honor that underpins his industry. Yet he doesn\'t put it together that it\'s the results of his life\'s poisonous work that killed his childhood friend in his barbershop, and turns to vengeance and anger instead. His obsession with Luke Cage and the failure of a major weapons deal undoes him despite all the protections he built around himself. Cottonmouth is a great character, played to almost "The Wire" levels of intensity by upcoming "Blade" star Mahershala Ali . The reason he\'s so low on this list? He\'s killed off halfway through the first season, and no other villain, not even Alfre Woodard as cousin Mariah Dillard, can measure up to the standard Ali set. Cottonmouth got a terrific send-off, but at too high a cost. 13. Alexandra Reid Netflix When defining a character, the game is to try and describe them without limiting them to physical attributes. Who are they? What are they driven by? What is their backstory? "The Defenders" set its lead villain role in the rich co-founder of the Hand, Alexandra Reid. She\'s played by Sigourney Weaver, who is given enough motivation to be an elegantly evil Sigourney Weaver. Unfortunately, that\'s pretty much it. Nominally, the quasi-immortal Reid has a connection to the exile of the Hand from K\'un-lun, turning there for solace and learning. It\'s a mere plot point, used to explain why she gives a matronly rip about the deceased Elektra, and the whole thing about K\'un-Lun\'s immortality elixir sets up why she suddenly has mortal motivations and gets to act like she\'s on a timer. She is. Otherwise, Alexandra looks fine as hell in a myriad of uptown stylings, with her hair on point and purring evilly in a way only Sigourney Weaver can. 12. Elektra Natchios Netflix It\'s a fact of Elektra\'s comics history that she has to die and return to torment her old friends and her lover, Matt Murdock. It\'s one of the most iconic events in comics, and for good reasons. But Elektra\'s appearances in "Daredevil," set before her inevitable demise, shouldn\'t have felt like she was on a bullet-train ride towards destiny. It\'s rough trying to build up a character whose pop culture impact relies on being killed, and actor Élodie Yung does her best with what she\'s given (which isn\'t much, although it\'s still way better than what the character was handed in 2005\'s "Elektra"). Her post-resurrection scenes are much better, showing off her feral, unrestrained ability and the depths of her barely-understood rage. It\'s good stuff, giving her final disappearance at the end of "The Defenders" real weight and meaning. Chronologically, we should still be the early years of Elektra\'s journey, so here\'s hoping she gets another chance to shine. 11. Trish Walker Netflix Trish spends her first few appearances in "Jessica Jones" setting herself up to be exactly what Jessica needs in a bestie. She\'s the \'90s teen movie Anne Hathaway to Jessica\'s emo girl, peppy and upbeat. Comic fans knew there could be potentially much more to Trish than that, based on her own history as the superhero Hellcat. The seeds of her future are laid in the first season, when she has a fling with the abusive and heavily altered Will Simpson. But Netflix had its own ideas for this all-new take on Walker, and although the series tells an effective story, it\'s also tragic stuff. Trish\'s journey is a bumpy ride. She does get the superpowers she seeks, but the cost to her psyche is high. She goes from joyful to vigilante hero to a terror in her own right. The Netflix era sees her a prisoner in the Raft, one of the few places where an empowered individual can be safely incarcerated. It\'d be a terrific place to jumpstart a new story for Trish Walker, leading to a potential return to heroism. 10. Madame Gao Netflix Marvel has gone through it when updating its heroes and villains to acknowledge the flaws in past storytelling, and its various tries, from the Ancient One to Xu Wenwu, reveal varying levels of success . The Netflix mini-universe didn\'t shy away from attempting to showcase a variety of Asian themes without resorting to bland stereotypes, and Madame Gao, an original character slightly based on the Crane Mother from the "Immortal Iron Fist" comics, is a solid try. Delightfully portrayed by Wai Ching Ho, Madame Gao leans into the elder mystic stereotype when it suits her. But she\'s one of the most ruthless leaders of the Hand, another near-immortal exile of K\'un-Lun who\'s first seen running the drug trade through Hell\'s Kitchen on "Daredevil." She\'s one of the most intriguing threads found in the Netflix universe, and it\'s a small shame that she joins the rest of the Hand in a final defeat in the climax of "The Defenders." We might not have seen a body, but we did probably see the last of this fascinating character. 9. Franklin \'Foggy\' Nelson Netflix There are moments during Netflix\'s "Daredevil" when one can forget the name of the show and think we\'re watching a drama about the misadventures of a well-meaning New York lawyer named Foggy Nelson. But Elden Henson is so fecklessly charming that the amount of focus he gets is entirely forgivable. Everyone, even the most devout, need a break from the deeper musings of Murdock\'s struggle with his Catholic fate, and Foggy is the guy who\'ll get the takeout and tell a story about the funniest way he\'s ever been shot down in a bar. Foggy is just a nice dude, and although his boundaries aren\'t as tight as they should be, it\'s both wrenching and necessary to watch him tell Matt where the line is. After popping up a variety of times throughout the Netflix universe, "Daredevil" sees him shoot for the moon in its final season, taking a shot at the district attorney\'s office. Though it doesn\'t pan out, it does pave the way for the law office of Nelson, Murdock, and Page to reopen. 8. Karen Page Netflix Karen Page could have been like some one-off "Law & Order" character that suddenly proves crucial when on the witness stand, and we\'re originally made to think of her pretty much like that. But she\'s dogged when she\'s curious, and she\'s made of hardier stuff than she lets on. Deborah Ann Woll is excellent at acting like the impressionable waif many take Karen Page for, but this young woman eventually turns herself into Frank Castle\'s moral center, much to his own surprise and dismay. Karen may be one of Daredevil\'s love interests in comics, but her dynamic with Frank is one of the best things to come out of the Netflix series. Not only does it give him an anchor to keep him sympathetic, but Karen comes out of his story stronger than ever. Like Foggy Nelson, but wiser, she finds her boundaries and sticks to them. With a return to the law office in her unfinished "Daredevil" future, it would be a delight to see her come back as she is, underestimated yet complicated. 7. Claire Temple Netflix Sometimes, in real life, we have someone that becomes the glue holding everyone else together, no matter the hurdles or the distance between us. It\'s that human connection that turns local New York nurse Claire Temple into the unlikely thread that connects almost the entire Netflix mini-universe. She\'s hardy and unflappable, empathetic without being anyone\'s doormat. Though she\'s based on a character from Luke Cage\'s "Hero for Hire" era, there\'s also a solid bit of the Night Nurse in her, the superhero-specialist medical professional who provides the basis for Claire\'s counterpart, Dr. Palmer, in "Doctor Strange." Rosario Dawson keeps Claire relatable. She\'s not a hero, but a tired young woman working a hard job. When the vigilante hijinks of one neighborhood begin to be too much for her, she goes elsewhere in the city, only to find the same struggles, and the same need for help. It\'s bittersweet that her relationship with Luke Cage is frayed by the end. Without Claire, it\'s not the same neighborhood anymore. But that\'s change, like it or not. 6. Wilson Fisk, the Kingpin Netflix Vincent D\'Onofrio is a wildly good character performer, the sort of fixture that\'s so competent and integral to the work that he often goes ironically forgotten in discussions of underrated actors. As Wilson Fisk, the intelligence, brutal anger, and paradoxical sweetness all combine to create a person we fear, hate, and even root for. Fisk is the sort of underworld criminal we can appreciate. He has a code of honor, and there\'s a method to his viciousness that makes him reasonable even when there\'s no doubt that he\'s on the shady side of being a true monster. There\'s logic to him, in defiance of real-world cruelty. Fisk, unlike many of the Netflix characters, is content to remain Daredevil\'s problem. Although he drifts through the same alleys as the Hand, his interests are specific and his ire is targeted. He has one weakness, his earnest love for Vanessa, the art gallery owner who charms him to his soul. Not to put too fine a point on it, but if D\'Onofrio doesn\'t get at least a voice cameo in "Spider-Man: No Way Home," it\'s a loss for Marvel as a whole. This is the best portrayal of Wilson Fisk to date, and we deserve more of him. 5. Kilgrave Netflix The original Purple Man is one of those daft \'60s comic characters whose first issues, by rights, should have ended up in the dusty bargain bins of history. And yet, once the potential terror of his ability was understood, decades later, writers began to use him effectively. He became a scarcely utilized horror, even manipulating a version of Cable to the edge of apocalypse. By ditching the purple skin and casting the boyishly charming David Tennant as this unlikely core villain of "Jessica Jones," Kilgrave became a monster that mattered. He\'s a supervillain, but he\'s all too real. As a normal-looking guy with an abnormal sense of humanity, Kilgrave becomes every gaslighting partner, every stalker, every attacker. He has nearly irresistible psychic control over his victims, but for many, that\'s only a metaphor for the very real power their abusers hold over them. That his grasp on Jessica feels like it lingers long after his death is equally powerful a metaphor. It doesn\'t cure the damage he did. But hey, it\'s a start. 4. Luke Cage Netflix Luke Cage, hero for hire, the protector of Harlem. It\'s a grim reflection, not a joke, that Black America needs bulletproof heroes to look up to. "Luke Cage" updates its eponymous hero from his Melvin Van Peebles-inspired origins into something that more closely reflects today\'s experiences. Luke\'s origin story, neighborhood, and group of friends comes to Netflix relatively whole, but what it all means is much more personal. First appearing in "Jessica Jones," Mike Colter\'s wry but determined take on Luke makes him the life of "The Defenders," a stable figure caught between the rest of the bickering team. Opinions on his fate in the final season of "Luke Cage" vary, and his role as the new keeper of Harlem\'s streets after the death of crime lord Mariah Dillard could go either way. It\'s an interesting place to leave Luke, and although Colter is currently enjoying success on the Paramount+ series "Evil," Luke Cage will always find a warm welcome home. 3. Frank Castle, the Punisher Netflix There\'s some willful mainstream ignorance about who the Punisher is and what he\'s about, but the nice thing about Gerry Conway, John Romita Sr., and Ross Andru\'s classic antihero is that he actively loathes that kind of ignorance. Frank Castle isn\'t an avatar for aggrieved and privileged Americans. He\'s a viral response to a diseased system. In a better world, his military wouldn\'t have abandoned him, his family wouldn\'t have been killed, and he wouldn\'t be on the streets, doing what he does. But this isn\'t that world, is it? Jon Bernthal gives Frank the seething sense of a wounded animal, but there\'s a calmer side to this version of the Punisher, too. His interactions with Karen Page remind him that he\'s human, if almost against his will, and that the things he does are violent and inhumane. We still have a lot of fondness for Thomas Jane in the 2004 film and the "Dirty Laundry" bootleg short , but Bernthal had a chance to explore who Frank was under the blood and anger, and the series did great by him. 2. Jessica Jones Netflix If Lisbeth Salander, the complicated star of "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo," was given superhero powers and some effective therapy, she\'d be Jessica Jones. Jessica, for all her flaws and self-destructive behavior — or perhaps, because of them — is someone we can understand and empathize with. She\'s in a crappy position. She\'s an unwilling superpower and an abuse survivor, and sometimes she\'s not really sure about who she is beyond all of that. Jessica is also someone that tries to do her best, even when she acts like she doesn\'t want to. It doesn\'t always work, and she takes her failures to heart. It\'s the kind of character that could come off edgelord emo all the time, but Krysten Ritter keeps Jessica grounded, funny, and human. The anger she always carries is tangible and well-earned, but it\'s also not always in control of her. Her last appearance sees her defy the ghost of Kilgrave and choose her own path, another step towards reclaiming her life. That\'s a major turn for Jessica. It\'s a shame we haven\'t yet seen what she could do next. 1. Matt Murdock, Daredevil Netflix Bringing Daredevil to life again after the sting of the 2003 Ben Affleck film was a risky endeavor for Netflix. Yes, the film isn\'t that bad, helped by a superior recut that hit DVD a year later. But "Daredevil" quickly set its own tone, with a grittier dive into Murdock\'s moral complexities and questions of faith. It\'s Netflix\'s "Iron Man," a surprise success that catapulted their corner of the Marvel franchise into something that fans identified as special. Charlie Cox, who had the talent to hit it big years ago, shines as the blind legal eagle with a weird night time hobby. Without him, the entire Netflix Marvel franchise falls into a dumpster. Instead, poor Matt falls into that dumpster repeatedly, as is his due, clambering out to delight us with another long-take fight in a hallway and to be Catholically tortured about how awesome he is. The weight of his actions is something he has to balance, and he doesn\'t always succeed. We could continue to wax lyrical about him, but look — experiencing his story is incomparable. Just watch it. Recommended']

Oscars Grammys Golden Globes Box Office Digital Magazines Exclusive ‘The Walking Dead’ at 15: Emmy-winning zombie maker Greg Nicotero on designing Bicycle Girl, Well Walker, and his other favorite monstrosities AMC\'s influential horror show originally premiered on Halloween night: Oct. 31, 2010. By Marcus James Dixon Plus icon Marcus James Dixon More stories by Marcus From ‘traumatized’ sidekick to ‘grown-up’ hero: Noah Schnapp reflects on his 10-year ‘Stranger Things’ journey 0 Comments Read more ‘Stranger Things 5’ reviews: It’s ‘still a hell of a ride,’ say critics, as the first 4 episodes hit Netflix 0 Comments Read more Matt and Ross Duffer tease Max’s fate in ‘Stranger Things 5’: ‘It’ll surprise people how she comes into the show’ 0 Comments Read more October 29, 2025 8:30 am The Walking \'s Greg Nicotero and colleague Greg Nicotero Share Share on Facebook Post google Google Preferred Pin it Show more sharing options Share to Flipboard Post to Tumblr Submit to Reddit Share on LinkedIn Share on WhatsApp Email Print This Page 0 One of the millions of fans who tuned in to watch the series premiere of The Walking Dead on Oct. 31, 2010 was Greg Nicotero . "I remember specifically watching it" on that Halloween night, he tells Gold Derby on the eve of the landmark zombie show\'s 15th anniversary. At the time, Nicotero was a special makeup effects artist, consulting producer, and second unit director. By the time the series was over, 11 seasons later, he had risen to the ranks of executive producer, directed almost 40 episodes, and won two Emmy Awards for Best Prosthetic Makeup, including for that inaugural season. Frank Darabont developed The Walking Dead for AMC based on Robert Kirkman \'s graphic novels, which debuted in 2003. The four showrunners were Darabont (Seasons 1-2), Glen Mazzara (Seasons 2-3), Scott M. Gimple (Seasons 4–8), and Angela Kang (Seasons 9–11). Notable cast members through the years included Andrew Lincoln as Rick Grimes, Norman Reedus as Daryl Dixon, Melissa McBride as Carol Peletier, Lauren Cohan as Maggie Greene, Danai Gurira as Michonne, and Jeffrey Dean Morgan as Negan — all of whom returned in various spin-offs. Related Stories Building the emotional architecture of ‘Hamnet’: An exclusive look at the Shakespearean production design 2026 Grammys Best Rap lineup shows that rumors of hip-hop’s death are greatly exaggerated Greg Nicotero, Andrew Lincoln, Norman Reedus Andrew Toth/Getty Images "Frank had wanted to do a zombie show for a long time, and he just never had the right material," Nicotero explains. Darabont\'s "sensibility of putting an ensemble cast together" was illustrated in his Stephen King adaptations The Shawshank Redemption , The Green Mile , and The Mist , and when Darabont "stumbled upon Kirkman\'s graphic novel," the filmmaker was able to put his own stamp on 1968\'s Night of the Living Dead . "And the rest is history." Nicotero reveals that, in the early days, "zombie stuff was really tricky, because it wasn\'t as mainstream as you would think." However, with the "advent of first-person video games" like The House of the Dead and Resident Evil , and filmmakers like Edgar Wright and Zack Snyder , the zombie genre all of a sudden became "elevated." The Walking Dead , however, was "a completely different animal," due to the fact that it was about "how these people are dealing with surviving." Nicotero notes, "It was always about survival. That\'s what Frank had said to me from day one. The zombie element of it is the cowboys and Indians sort of motif. Frank\'s sensibility with an ensemble cast, and just his vision for the show, made it much more accessible. Was it gory? Yeah, of course it was ... but there was a sense of humanity." Nicotero highlights three early examples of The Walking Dead at its most humane: Rick apologizing to the legless "Bicycle Girl" zombie before killing her, Lennie James \' Morgan struggling with "shooting his wife," and Laurie Holden \'s Andrea "cradling her dead sister," played by Emma Bell . "I think those scenes, among many, just redefined how people gravitated to this kind of material." Despite creating thousands of walkers for the various iterations of the show over the past 15 years, Nicotero has never stopped thinking about "Bicycle Girl." "This one is my favorite, for sure," he readily admits. "It was the first image that AMC released from the show, and people were like, \'How the f--k did they do that?\' I look at a lot of the footage that I\'ve shot over the years, and what a sheer delight it was to be a part of the show from the beginning. It changed my life, without a doubt." When Darabont asked him if he wanted to direct an episode in Season 2, the makeup wizard was initially caught off-guard. "Frank said, \'You\'ve directed second unit for me on The Mist , and you\'ve done short films, and you\'re ready to go.\'" But then, Nicotero recalls being asked the following "trick question": "Do you want a zombie-light episode or a zombie-heavy episode?" Since Nicotero already knew how to direct the creatures, he requested a character piece that would "challenge [him] to work with the actors, and tell a story." He ended up taking the reins on Episode 11 of Season 2, titled "Judge, Jury, Executioner," where Jeffrey DeMunn \'s Dale was killed. "There\'s one zombie in the whole episode," Nicotero says proudly. "That episode is like 12 Angry Men , where they\'re all sitting around in Hershel\'s [ Scott Wilson ] farm, trying to decide what to do with this hostage, Randall [ Michael Zegen ], that they found," he recalls. "Should they let him go, or should they kill him? That was the first episode I ever directed, and almost 40 episodes later, it continues to be an amazing experience." Nicotero firmly believes that "the first six seasons are untouchable." He specifically praises "the quality of the writing, the acting, and the storytelling," adding, "I would read the scripts, and I couldn\'t wait to get the next one. I had two young children at the time, and I think at one point, I actually put the scripts down and went and hugged my kids. My son was the exact same age that Chandler Riggs [as Carl Grimes] was when we shot the show, and it was so moving." One of the most-talked about creatures over the years has been the "Well Walker," which Nicotero crafted after Darabont had the idea for "this zombie that is trapped in a well and becomes bloated, and as they\'re pulling it out, it tears in half." Being a producer on the show allowed Nicotero to "get an advanced look at the scripts, so that we could begin prepping the creature effects and the gags much earlier than we would have been on a normal show." It took his team "six weeks to build," which was a blessing because if he hadn\'t been "privy to the scripts," they would have probably only had about 12 days. A zombie is born Scott Garfield/AMC In addition to his two Emmy wins for The Walking Dead in 2011 and 2012, Nicotero took home trophies for Dune in 2001 and The Pacific in 2010, and was nominated for Breaking Bad and Fallout . "You never set out thinking that you\'re going to win an award, because that\'s not what it\'s about," he declares. "You do it because you love it. You do it because you want the audience to experience something that they have never experienced or seen before. And I think The Walking Dead is a real testament to that." Nicotero is the creator, host, and executive producer of Guts & Glory , the competition horror series airing now on Shudder and AMC+. He calls the experience "a lot of fun," adding, "I\'m a big competition reality show fan. I love Survivor , The Traitors , The Amazing Race , Hell\'s Kitchen , Top Chef , Big Brother ... I don\'t know how I have time to watch them all!" Greg Nicotero, \'Guts and Glory\' AMC/Shudder The original concept for Guts & Glory was to "meld a competition show and a horror movie." Enter the horror-based challenges, like an autopsy, being buried alive, zombies, monsters, and even a possession. He notes, "It has never been done before, and it was a tremendous amount of fun." The two-episode finale airs Nov. 4. Nicotero concludes, "Halloween has replaced Christmas as the greatest holiday ever invented. People celebrate it for two months at a time, and when it\'s over, there\'s a palpable sadness — especially in my line of work." And for the record, his favorite horror films are Steven Spielberg \'s Jaws ("I did the restoration of the shark that\'s at the Academy Museum") and George A. Romero \'s Dawn of the Dead ("It was the movie that made me want to do makeup effects"). When it comes to Western TV, there is almost an endless number of shows to choose from. But if shows like Gunsmoke , Bonanza , or Rawhide — which each have a couple hundred episodes — are a bit too daunting, there\'s another trail you could wander down. Westerns, especially those that air on television, come in all shapes and sizes. While there are certainly long-running horse operas out there, some of the easiest binges are the quick two-season programs, full of galloping gunplay . When it comes to two-season Westerns, there are plenty to choose from. From the \'50s and \'60s to modern day, traditional horse operas to neo-Westerns, there\'s a bingeable series out there for everyone. Some were canceled on cliffhangers before their time while others tell complete tales of the great outdoors and the wild frontier — but all are worth revisiting. So, without further ado, here are some two-season TV Westerns that make for easy binging . 11 \'1923\' (2022-2025) Harrison Ford as Jacob Dutton beside Helen Mirren as Cara Dutton holding rifles in snow in 1923 Season 2. Image via Paramount+ The second prequel to Taylor Sheridan \'s flagship Yellowstone drama, 1923 tells the story of Jacob ( Harrison Ford ) and Clara Dutton ( Helen Mirren ) as they fight to keep their family\'s homestead from falling into the hands of a greedy business tycoon. If that sounds a bit too similar to the aforementioned Kevin Costner series, 1923 tells a concise and complete tale that extends beyond just Jacob and Clara and their Montana-based war . On the other side of the globe, their nephew, Spencer ( Brandon Sklenar ) falls in love with British socialite Alex ( Julia Schlaepfer ) as they travel the world together. 1923 is set during Montana\'s Depression, which hit a decade before the nationwide Great Depression, overlapping with the Prophibition-era. In two seasons and 16 episodes, Sheridan gives greater context to the Dutton family story , with 1923 surpassing Yellowstone in most respects . With an engaging set of characters and a more condensed plot than some of Sheridan\'s other television dramas, this prequel series is a unique take on the genre that shouldn\'t be slept on. Just a quick note, viewer discretion is definitely advised... 10 \'The Californians\' (1957-1959) Jack (Sean McClory) and Martha McGivern (Nan Leslie) talk with Dion Patrick (Adam Kennedy) on \'The Californians\' Image via NBC Long before Saturday Night Live poked fun at those from California, NBC\'s The Californians placed the spotlight on Gold Rush-era San Francisco. In an age where most Westerns followed lawmen or gunslingers in traditional Old West towns like Dodge City or Tombstone, this two-season drama centered (at first) on a band of vigilantes , including Adam Kennedy \'s Dion Patrick, who aimed to take back their town from the corrupt government officials. Over time, the series morphed into a more traditional Western series, with Richard Coogan \'s Matthew Wayne taking over, but the series wasn\'t meant to last. Back in the \'50s, television seasons lasted a lot longer than what we\'re used to these days. The Californians \' two seasons add up to 69 episodes total , so this is a bit longer of a binge than some of the other entries on the list. Of course, each episode runs less than 30 minutes, so they go by pretty quickly by comparison. For a Western series with a non-traditional setting (1850s California) and plenty of fun, add The Californians to your list. 9 \'Broken Arrow\' (1956-1958) Michael Ansara as Cochise and John Lupton as Tom Jeffords in the television adaptation of \'Broken Arrow.\' Image via ABC Based on the James Stewart film of the same name, Broken Arrow premiered on ABC a few years after the feature hit theaters. But instead of Stewart in the leading role, John Lupton took over as Indian Agent Tom Jeffords, who — along with Michael Ansara \'s Cochise — fought to keep the peace between the white settlers and the Apache people. At a time when nuance concerning Native American issues wasn\'t exactly popular, Broken Arrow was ( just like the original film ) a trailblazer in the genre . Like The Californians , Broken Arrow \'s two seasons include far more episodes than what we\'ve grown accustomed to in the 21st century. This half-hour Western program boasts 72 episodes total , balancing Lupton\'s Jeffords and Ansara\'s Cochise as leading men equal on all accounts. Not only did each man learn from one another, but the series offered a balanced understanding of the Old West that blended two differing cultures. 8 \'Hec Ramsey\' (1972-1974) Richard Boone as Hec Ramsey stares down a gun in \'Hec Ramsey\' Image via NBC After Richard Boone spent years dazzling viewers as Paladin on Have Gun — Will Travel , he returned to the genre in 1972 for a non-traditional take on the genre, Hec Ramsey . As a part of the NBC Sunday Mystery Movie programming block, the Boone-led drama follows the titular lawman as he uses newfound scientific techniques to investigate crimes . Think NCIS but in the Old West . With extended episodes that are essentially made-for-TV movies, Hec Ramsey was, in more ways than one, ahead of its time. For fans of Boone\'s previous six-season Western, the two-season Hec Ramsey will feel like a return to form, at least in some respects. Boone considered Hec to be something of a continuation of Paladin, albeit with a new backstory and different outlook on life. With 10 different 90-minute to 2-hour episodes to choose from , Hec Ramsey is great for those hoping for something more feature-length but still distinctly TV. 7 \'Dead Man\'s Gun\' (1997-1999) A raving preacher (Tim Matheson) holds the titular gun in the Western anthology series \'Dead Man\'s Gun.\' Image via Showtime Western anthologies were once a dime a dozen, but by the late \'90s, the genre no longer saturated television the way it once had. Nevertheless, Showtime\'s Dead Man\'s Gun stood out as a Twilight Zone -esque take on the genre , where each episode followed a poor unfortunate soul haunted by the titular firearm . As the mystical gun would fall from one hand to the next, tragedy (and death) went wherever it did, and the Old West felt like a much darker place. Dead Man\'s Gun dealt with issues of human nature, as the gun enhanced its wielder\'s worst characteristics. For two seasons, the anthology — created by Ed Spielman and Howard Spielman — was hosted by Kris Kristofferson , who dissected the lives of characters played by Henry Winkler , John Glover , Graham Greene , Laurie Holden , and plenty of others. Even better, after 44 episodes, the series ends with the weapon returning to its maker : the Grime Reaper himself. 6 \'Outer Range\' (2022-2024) Josh Brolin as Royal Abbott and Lili Taylor as Cecilia Abbott in \'Outer Range\' Season 2. Image via Prime Video If Dead Man\'s Gun only whet your whistle concerning "Weird Westerns," then the psychedelic mind trip that is Prime Video\'s Outer Range is the obvious next step . After Wyoming rancher Royal Abbott ( Josh Brolin ) finds a mysterious black hole in the middle of his west pasture, things around their small town go from bad to worse. If time travel isn\'t your thing, then Outer Range may not be for you. Admittedly, it\'s the weirdest show on this list, being both a neo-Western and a more traditional Western at times, but it\'s also one of the most imaginative. Fair warning: after two seasons and 15 episodes, Outer Range was canceled on a major cliffhanger , and it\'s unlikely that it will ever be resolved ( though it definitely deserves another season ). So, watch this one at your own risk — but definitely consider giving it a shot because it\'s an incredible series with a great cast that also includes Lili Taylor , Imogen Poots , Lewis Pullman , and Tom Pelphrey . It\'s an oddball neo-Western, but it\'ll have your head spinning in the best ways. 5 \'The Rebel\' (1959-1961) Nick Adams as Johnny Yuma on a promotional picture for \'The Rebel\' Image via ABC With a killer theme song by Johnny Cash , The Rebel was a Western program that followed former Confederate soldier Johnny Yuma ( Nick Adams ) as he did the typical horse opera dance by wandering from town to town, job to job, and adventure to adventure. The series even tackled the basic plot of The Hateful Eight long before Quentin Tarantino helmed the film. Johnny Yuma was one of those Western protagonists who was too cool for school, even if his program was canceled too early due to excessive violence — though, don\'t be fooled by that statement, compared to something like 1923 , it\'s child\'s play. Like the aforementioned Western dramas that began back in the late \'50s, two seasons of Johnny Yuma equals 76 episodes to binge through . But The Rebel was a half-hour program, so if you\'re thinking in terms of 42-minute shows, you\'ve only really got half of that to watch through. Either way, you\'ll find yourself lost in The Rebel , which will keep you well-entertained the whole adventure. 4 \'Lancer\' (1968-1970) Wayne Maunder as Scott Lancer and James Stacy as Johnny Madrid Lancer in \'Lancer\' Image via CBS Speaking of Tarantino, if you\'re at all familiar with his work on Once Upon a Time In Hollywood , then you\'ve probably heard of Lancer in passing. It\'s the show where Leonardo DiCaprio \'s Rick Dalton gets cast as the villain after his own fictitious series was axed by the network. Well, long before Timothy Olyphant and Luke Perry pretended to play Lancer \'s leading men, James Stacy and Wayne Maunder tackled the roles of half-brothers Johnny Madrid Lancer and Scott Lancer , who, along with their father Murdoch ( Andrew Duggan ), sought to protect their land from invading forces on all sides. Compared to some of the other two-season Westerns on this list, Lancer has long been forgotten by most . Nevertheless, this hour-long program raked up 51 episodes in its day , so it\'s, admittedly, the longest binge on this list. When you consider it\'s about as long as Yellowstone , and follows a similar basic plot, you may as well take a stab at the lesser-known \'60s classic. 3 \'The Son\' (2017-2019) Pierce Brosnan as Eli McCullough wearing a grey vest and holding a gun in \'The Son.\' Image via Sonar Entertainment For a Western journey that expands on multiple time periods and follows both older and younger versions of some of its leading characters , AMC\'s The Son may be the right two-season binge for you. Featuring Pierce Brosnan as ranching patriarch Eli McCullough, the show largely centers around him as he seeks to not just save his family\'s cattle empire, but secure the oil beneath his neighbor\'s land as well. The show largely takes place in 1915, but the flashback plotline to young Eli\'s ( Jacob Lofland ) life with the Comanche takes the show back to the 1850s. If multi-generational tales about Texas ranching and survival (not to mention the mythic way Western legends are preserved) are your bag of tea, then you\'ll find plenty to love about The Son . Spanning two seasons and 20 episodes, The Son tells a complete story from beginning to end as Brosnan shows how truly capable he is at leading such a complicated venture — one far more satisfying than Yellowstone . 2 \'Joe Pickett\' (2021-2023) Image via Paramount+ If neo-Westerns like Longmire or Justified are more your speed, then you ought to consider Joe Pickett . A Spectrum Original turned to Paramount+, this two-season series is based on the popular mystery thrillers by C.J. Box , with Michael Dorman bringing the titular Wyoming game warden to life. As Joe spends each season tackling a new mystery, you\'ll be instantly drawn to his do-good personality and the sweet family he fights for. This one may be set in modern day, but it feels just as Western as they come. After two seasons and 20 episodes total, Joe Pickett was unceremoniously canceled by Paramount+ . The good news is that each season-long mystery is always wrapped up by the end. The bad news is that there are a few loose ends that never got tied up. But don\'t let that stop you, because Joe Pickett is one of those neo-Westerns that, just like the novels it\'s based on, you won\'t be able to turn off. Google is updating how content is shown.
