Home TV and Film Where are the cast of ‘70s sitcoms now? From M*A*S*H and Happy Days to The Partridge Family and The Brady Bunch, what happened to the stars of the disco era’s biggest sitcoms? © Disney General Entertainment Con Romy Journee Audience Writer November 5, 2025 Nov 5, 2025, 6:02 PM GMT Share this: It’s hard to pick just one of your favourite sitcoms from the ‘70s – the decade brought us so many cult classics that are still widely watched and loved today, from the wartime antics of M*A*S*H to the endlessly quotable The Brady Bunch . Amidst all the fond memories of watching re-runs of these hit shows on cable TV, you may be wondering what happened to the stars who headlined these shows , and the direction their careers took after the sitcoms wrapped. If you’re wondering what became of the original Marcia Brady, the legendary matriarch of The Partridge Family , or the big-name star from Happy Days who went on to win an Oscar , then wonder no more. We’re taking a look at some of the biggest names from ‘70s sitcoms, what they got up to after their shows ended, and where they are now… © CBS via Getty Images,FilmMagic Sally will appear in the upcoming Gilmore Girls documentary Sally Struthers – All in the Family While Gilmore Girls fans like myself will recognise Sally Struthers as the raspy-voiced Babette, the star first shot to fame as Archie and Edith’s daughter Gloria Stivic in All in the Family (1971–1979), a role which she won two Emmys for. In a moment of serendipity, Sally auditioned for the sitcom after being fired from The Tim Conway Comedy Hour in New York, telling People executives said she made the show look “cheap”. She went on to reprise her iconic role in the self-titled Gloria (1982–1983). Sally is currently appearing in Netflix ’s comedy hit A Man on the Inside (2024–) opposite Ted Danson , who stars as a retiree-turned-private investigator – which sounds perfect for The Thursday Murder Club fans. The actress will also appear in the upcoming Gilmore Girls documentary Drink Coffee, Talk Fast , in celebration of the show’s 25th anniversary. © Getty Images Alan\'s hit film is now a Netflix series Alan Alda – M*A*S*H The beating heart of the wartime sitcom, Alan Alda’s portrayal of Captain Benjamin Franklin "Hawkeye" Pierce is still legendary to this day. Whether he was pranking Frank Burns or sharing a drink with B.J. Hunnicut, Alan’s delivery of the character\'s quips and witty one-liners brought the role to life, scoring him eleven Emmy nominations and two wins. The star continued to have a prolific career following M*A*S*H , portraying Senator Arnold Vinick in The West Wing (1999–2006) and earning his first Academy Award nomination for Martin Scorsese’s The Aviator (2004). Still ruling screens at 89-years-old, Alan most recently appeared in an episode of Netflix’s The Four Seasons (2025–), Tina Fey ’s TV adaptation of his hit 1981 movie – which he not only starred in, but wrote and directed! © Getty Images The star reunited with her Brady family to renovate the original house from the sitcom Maureen McCormick – The Brady Bunch Marcia, Marcia, Marcia… forever the queen bee of the legendary sitcom family, much to the chagrin of Jan, Maureen McCormick was the original eldest Brady daughter in The Brady Bunch (1969–1974). After worming her way into viewers’ hearts with a flick of her signature blonde locks, Maureen went on to reprise the role in the plethora of Brady spin-offs, from The Brady Brides (1981) to A Very Brady Christmas (1988). After publishing her bestselling autobiography Here’s the Story (2008), Maureen continued gracing screens, turning her hand to reality TV, with appearances on shows like I’m a Celebrity … and Dancing with the Stars . The star even joined her former castmates for A Very Brady Renovation (2019), which turned the iconic exterior Brady house into an interior-perfect replica of the beloved TV home, which Maureen revealed to People she visits frequently as part of her charity work. You may also like The cast of iconic ‘80s Sitcoms: Where are they now? The mixed fortunes of 1960s sitcom stars – from Bewitched to I Dream of Jeannie What happened to these 1970s TV show stars? © Bettmann Archive,WireImage Bea ruled the sitcom scene for decades Bea Arthur – Maude Before she was Dorothy Zbornak on The Golden Girls (1985–1992), Bea Arthur joined Sally Struthers on All in the Family before her character – after just two episodes – earned her own spin-off series, Maude (1972–1978). The liberal foil to her cousin-in-law Archie, CBS reportedly wanted a show centered on a strong, independent female lead, and saw endless potential in both Maude and the actress who portrayed her. After decades on top of the sitcom scene, the star continued to make regular appearances on comedy shows and documentaries up until her death in 2009, with her last credited role being in Curb Your Enthusiasm (2005). An inimitable star of both stage and screen, Bea also holds the record for the third most nominations for the Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Comedy Series, behind Mary Tyler Moore and Julia Louis-Dreyfus . © Bettmann Archive,Getty Images Ron\'s new film Eden is out now Ron Howard – Happy Days A child actor who shot to fame in The Andy Griffith Show (1960–1968), Ron Howard is arguably best known for his role as Richie Cunningham in the popular sitcom Happy Days (1974–1980). After seven seasons of causing mischief with Fonzie, Ralph, and Potsie, Ron retired his pen and paper to pursue a career as a director after his debut with Grand Theft Auto (1977), and went on to win the Academy Awards for Best Director and Best Picture for A Beautiful Mind (2001) A father of four – including actress Bryce Dallas Howard – Ron is still very active in the film scene, with recent credits including Netflix’s Hillbilly Elegy (2020) and Eden (2024) starring Jude Law and Sydney Sweeney . The star also revealed to People he still has a text thread with his Happy Days co-stars Don Most, Anson Williams, and Henry Winkler , calling the quarter’s friendship “one of the really great gifts of my adult life”. © Getty Images,WireImage From Oklahoma! to this classic sitcom, Shirley is musical royalty Shirley Jones – The Partridge Family The music-loving matriarch of The Partridge Family (1970–1974), Shirley Jones already had a successful musical career after starring in the likes of Oklahoma! (1955) and Carousel (1956). As the widow Shirley Partridge, who forms a pop band with her five kids, Shirley received both critical acclaim and praise from her co-stars, described as “one of the best human beings I’ve ever known” by actor David Cassidy, her on-screen son and real-life stepson. After a lifetime as the ultimate triple threat, Shirley has taken a step back from showbiz, but starred in a production of The Music Man in 2012 after leading the cast of the 1962 film edition. If you still can’t get enough of the Broadway star’s melodic voice, the star’s album A Touch of Christmas will no doubt perfectly soundtrack the upcoming festive season. © Radio Times via Getty Images,PA Images via Getty Images Connie shared the sweetest words about her late co-star Prunella Scales Connie Booth – Fawlty Towers One half of the mastermind writing duo behind Fawlty Towers (1975–1979) – alongside her then-husband John Cleese – Connie Booth went on to star in the hit sitcom as Polly Sherman, the hotel’s level-headed maid. After four years of penning the hit series and mediating no end of squabbles between Basil and Sybil, Connie continued acting up until her last appearance in BBC’s The Buccaneers (1995) as Jackie March. Connie ended up trading her life in the spotlight for one as a psychotherapist, a career she held until her retirement. She’s also been happily married to former New Yorker drama critic John Lahr since 2000. The star shared a touching tribute to her late co-star, Prunella Scales, with Radio Times , writing: “"As a performer Prunella was memorable; it\'s part of life\'s irony that over time she lost her memory. But even there, she had the capacity to turn bleakness into something bright. \'I can\'t remember everything,\' she said, \'but I can still remember to laugh\'." © CBS via Getty Images,Getty Images Ed earned five Emmys for his portrayal of Lou Grant Ed Asner – The Mary Tyler Moore Show The gruff yet lovable news director in The Mary Tyler Moore Show (1970–1977), Lou Grant was the perfect foil to Mary Richard’s sunny optimism, and Ed Asner quickly made a name for himself as one of the show’s leading stars. He went on to earn his own spin-off, Lou Grant (1977–1982), and ended up earning a staggering five Emmys – all for playing the role of Lou. The star ended up going from strength to strength after the sitcom wrapped, starring in ABC’s Thunder Alley (1994–1995) and voicing J. Jonah Jameson in Spider-Man: The Animated Series (1994–1998). Ed passed away in 2021 at age 91, appearing posthumously in several roles including the Halloween special Muppets Haunted Mansion (2021). © CBS via Getty Images,Getty Images Marla is 94 and still acting Marla Gibbs – The Jeffersons Marla Gibbs made her sitcom debut in The Jeffersons (1975–1980) as Florence Johnston, George’s sassy and sarcastic maid, and went on to receive five Emmy Award nominations. Her success on the show earned her the role of Mary Jenkins in 227 (1985–1990), which chronicled the lives of Black women living together in Washington, D.C. – a show created specifically for Marla, who had starred in the production in Los Angeles. After achieving sitcom notoriety – she also co-produced 227 and sang the theme song – Marla appeared in films like The Brothers (2001) and Madea’s Witness Protection (2012) opposite Eugene Levy and Denise Richards. She’s also a familiar face in Shondaland, having guest starred on both Grey’s Anatomy (2022) and its spin-off Station 19 (2018). At 94-years-old, Marla revealed at the American Black Film Festival Honours in 2025 that she’s “ready to do some more roles!” © Getty Images Cindy shared some heartfelt words about her co-star Penny Marshall Cindy Williams – Laverne & Shirley The sweet and perky foil to tomboy Laverne Defazio, Shirley Feeney was one half of the hit Happy Days spin-off Laverne & Shirley (1976–1983), which followed two best friends living together in the ‘50s and working at a brewery in Milwaukee. Cindy’s chemistry with Laverne’s actress Penny Marshall earned them both critical acclaim, and the sitcom was praised for its unique dynamic, centering on two female friends and offering an image of womanhood seldom seen on TV. After guest roles in the 2000s on shows like Law & Order: Special Victims Unit (2004) and Sam & Cat (2013), and making her Broadway debut in The Drowsy Chaperone (2007), Cindy passed away in 2023 , five years after her co-star Penny. Prior to her passing, Cindy reflected on Penny’s death, telling People her co-star was “utterly unique” that she “can\'t describe how I\'ll miss her”. Now, the film has roared at the top of the Peacock chart on its streaming debut. Jurassic World Rebirth left behind the past many ways, ditching legacy characters and, as the title suggested, pumping new life into the franchise with Scarlett Johansson and Mahershala Ali leading a brand new cast of characters venturing to a dinosaur-infested island. While critics continued to point out its “charmless, plotless, sloppy” faults, audiences continued to fill theaters and show that there is nothing extinct about the Jurassic saga yet. The story this time around goes a little like this: “Five years after the events of Jurassic World Dominion, the planet\'s ecology has proven largely inhospitable to dinosaurs. Those remaining exist in isolated equatorial environments with climates resembling the one in which they once thrived. The three most colossal creatures within that tropical biosphere hold the key to a drug that will bring miraculous life-saving benefits to humankind.” In the end, a Jurassic movie lives and dies with its thrills and dinosaur effects, and audiences found more than enough of both to give the film a 71% score on Rotten Tomatoes, higher than the more divided 50% rating from critics. However, it is the $868 million box office that really hits home just how popular the franchise continues to be, and that is why another movie is already on the way . \'Jurassic World Rebirth 2\' Is Reportedly in Development Universal Pictures While completely rebooting the Jurassic franchise, leaving behind the Chris Pratt and Bryce Dallas Howard era so soon after Jurassic World: Dominion , was perhaps a risky strategy, it seems to have paid off. According to reports back in September, Johansson is wanted back as the lead for another movie, but there has been little information about whether Gareth Edwards has been approached to return as director, or whether any of the other stars – the ones whose characters were not eaten – could also be returning. Jurassic World Rebirth had one ace up its sleeve that a sequel will not have, as it was able to realize the final set-piece scene from Michael Crichton’s original novel that had not been used in previous movies: the river raft scene . Following the adventure with mutant dinosaurs, where the next Jurassic movie will go is unclear. We have had dinosaurs being created and sold on the black market, dinosaurs being medical saviors, and dinosaurs being planned for use as weapons. Although the latter of these has only been hinted at, the next movie could find weaponized dinosaurs being a big plot point and could end up being one of the few ways the franchise could expand without it simply being another story about people running from prehistoric beasts on an island. Night Shyamalan’s once-maligned 2004 thriller. Now, that’s par for the course with Shyamalan. Trap , Old , and especially The Lady in the Water remain polarizing genre pictures. They have plenty of fans, but just as many detractors. The spark for this burgeoning classic came from film journalist Brandon Streussnig ( @BrndnStrssng ), who posted on X: “Rewatched The Village last night, sorta solidified itself into M Night’s upper echelon for me, but man, the scene where Ivy is searching for Lucius’s hand amidst the chaos of the village trying to find who Noah stabbed f*cked me up BAD. Maybe the most moving thing he’s done.” The post was later quoted by writer Shea Serrano, who called for a “critical reevaluation” of the film. Suddenly, everyone was weighing in on the movie that, nearly two decades ago, critics dismissed as a major disaster. When The Village debuted in 2004, Roger Ebert gave it one star , calling it a “colossal miscalculation,” though he admitted Shyamalan was “a director of considerable skill who evokes stories out of moods.” A.O. Scott at The New York Times was harsher . He called out the film’s “ridiculousness” and accused Shyamalan of having “sloppy and obvious” ideas. The Village tells the story of the inhabitants of an isolated 19th-century village. They live in fear of the red-cloaked creatures in the surrounding woods. When Lucius Hunt (Joaquin Phoenix) is stabbed by another villager out of jealousy, Elder Edward Walker (William Hurt) sends his blind daughter, Ivy (Bryce Dallas Howard), to gather life-saving medications from one of the towns just beyond the woods. It’s a dangerous task, but Edward believes she’s the only one who can do it. Watch the trailer below: I was eight when it came out. I remember watching it in high school Sociology class (of all places) and being struck by how sad it was. Like The Sixth Sense (1999), The Village is a deeply emotional movie about grief, isolation, and the lengths people go to protect themselves. It reminds me a lot of the short story, “The Red Bow” by George Saunders, which was published in 2003 (it’s no surprise that both of these came out after the September 11th attacks). In the midst of the ongoing Shyamalan renaissance (fueled in part by 2024’s Trap , a film I personally think is near-perfect), it feels like the right moment to reconsider The Village . Shyamalan may not always get it right, and yes, some of his movies are kind of silly , but he’s one of the few mainstream directors still committed to telling original, entertaining stories right now. Night Shyamalan , it\'s not usually romance that comes to mind, but that\'s where he\'s headed next. A master of plot twists , the one he\'s pulled this time is something his fans never saw coming, having recently wrapped production on Remain , a supernatural thriller that he wrote with none other than Nicholas Sparks . Both of them are accomplished names in their respective areas, but their team-up is surely unexpected, given how seemingly distant their preferred genres are, with Shyamalan being a master of modern horror and suspense, and Sparks one of the most successful romance writers this century. They have more in common than audiences would think, though, and their partnership sounds like a match made in heaven — or, in Remain \'s case, whatever comes after death. ‘Remain’ Marks M. Night Shyamalan and Nicholas Sparks’ First-Ever Collaboration M Night Shyamalan and Paul Giamatti sat outside on some deckchairs in Lady in the Water Image Via Buena Vista Pictures The premise for Remain feels closer to Sparks than Shyamalan at first, but it was actually the latter\'s own original concept. Speaking to the Los Angeles Times , Sparks revealed that he and Shyamalan have admired each other\'s work for a long time, and their partnership began thanks to a suggestion of the writer\'s team, with Shyamalan reaching out shortly after. They decided to develop a project together and met a few times to spitball ideas, each coming up with an original concept. Sparks says that the idea of a "supernatural romance" came from Shyamalan , as his own idea "was pretty dark." The story follows grieving architect Tate Donovan ( Jake Gyllenhaal ), who has recently been discharged from a mental institution to treat his severe depression following the loss of his sister. Looking for a fresh start, he travels to Cape Cod to stay at a bed-and-breakfast, where he ends up meeting a mysterious but charming girl named Wren ( Phoebe Dynevor ). Tate is generally a grounded and skeptical individual, with his sister having always been the one who believed in more than reason could explain. Now, Wren coming into his life will test the limits of his beliefs in some rather "otherworldly" ways. As part of their collaboration, Remain was also recently released as a novel penned by Sparks and became an instant bestseller . Although they are part of the same project, Sparks promises surprises for those who\'ve read the book when the movie comes out. For it to work as a novel, he\'d have to "tweak some things," according to the writer. “I would call him and say, ‘Can I make the ending different?’ or ‘How about this twist instead?’” So, even those who\'ve read the book may very well be in for a few surprises when Shyamalan\'s movie, which he wrote, directed, and produced, comes out. But we\'d expect nothing less from the master of the plot twist. Shyamalan and Sparks Have More in Common as Storytellers Than People Expect As weird as this team-up may seem, Shyamalan and Sparks clicked almost immediately, with the latter saying their collaboration "came down to chemistry." Shyamalan\'s stories may attract viewers due to his plot twists and mastery in building tension, but they are also rooted in their protagonists\' deep emotional core . Shyamalan has given us several compelling protagonists in his films, from Bruce Willis \' Malcolm Crowe in The Sixth Sense and Bryce Dallas Howard \'s Ivy in The Village , to even making his central character an antagonist with his last film, Trap . Posts By Makuochi Echebiri Apr 23, 2025 Sparks usually works the same way, building chemistry between his characters by developing them from an emotional standpoint. Noah ( Ryan Gosling ) and Allie\'s ( Rachel McAdams ) saga in The Notebook , for example, is only that impactful because we know who they are and what their feelings are deep down, similar to the characters in Message in a Bottle and A Walk to Remember . Those are all tragedies as much as romances , leaving anyone with a heart in shambles upon watching their adaptations. For Remain , the core emotional theme seems to be grief, which both Shyamalan and Sparks regularly integrate into their work. It has been a recurring theme in many series and films in recent years, often explored as a kind of love that lingers after we lose a loved one — a feeling that, well, "remains" despite their departure. A love story with a supernatural twist feels like an amalgamation of the types of stories Shyamalan and Sparks excel at . Shyamalan Almost Collaborated With Sparks in \'The Notebook,\' Too Another interesting thing about Remain is that it was almost the second collaboration between Shyamalan and Sparks. That\'s because, as Sparks revealed, when The Notebook was being developed as a feature film back in the late 1990s, the producers initially sought Shyamalan to write the script . It didn\'t work, as he chose to focus on The Sixth Sense instead, but it seems like the door was left open on both ends for them to eventually team up in the future. Of course, it worked for the best, as both movies went on to become hits. Back then, Shyamalan had already worked as a writer, albeit uncredited , on She\'s All That , so it was already clear he knew how to tackle romances. So, Remain feels like a full-circle moment for a collaboration that was decades in the works, and will hopefully pay off with another hit. Remain hits theaters on October 23, 2026. In fact, the vitriol that is often leveled at these epic movies is often far more substantial than that reserved for smaller or less ambitious films, likely due to the antipathy for them being made equivalent to the size of the movies themselves. While the kinds of epic films released in the last ten years don't resemble the same output from prior decades, with bloated CGI action-adventure epics usurping many of the more traditional historical epics in the release schedule, the inconsistent quality certainly has. The worst epics from the last ten years represent a full spectrum of the subgenre. There are bland historical epics, bloated sci-fi epics, flaccid franchises, and overindulgent passion projects. While some may have turned a tidy profit at the box office, none were well-liked by critics or audiences, with the most positively received being divisive at best. Even the individual elements that are well executed are lost amid the long runtimes of their respective mediocre films. They might have had ambition, but t hese eight epic films from the last ten years all ended up being a big waste of time . 8 'Ben Hur' (2016) Two men race each other in horse-drawn chariots in an arena in Ben Hur (2016). Image via Paramount Pictures This ill-advised remake of the classic 1959 biblical epic starring Charlton Heston does nothing new or interesting with the source material and pales in every way in comparison to the previous film , especially in its recreation of the iconic chariot race sequence. The use of CGI and more modern quick-cut editing techniques leaves all the film's action feeling lifeless. In between those sequences, the plotline of revenge, set against the backdrop of the Roman Empire in the time of Jesus Christ, is exceedingly by-the-numbers. The underwritten material strands an otherwise talented cast, including star Jack Huston , whose short-lived bid for leading man status ended with this film. 2016's Ben-Hur was a major flop at the box office, failing to even entice the often lucrative faith-based crowd. It was one of a number of large-scale ancient historical epics made in the 2010s that failed spectacularly at the box office, precipitating a major drop in interest in the subgenre. Sword-and-sandals movies have always been a gamble at the box office, even for battle-tested filmmakers like Ridley Scott , whose own Exodus: Gods and Kings crashed and burned only two years before. Milquetoast efforts like this remake are a big part of the reason why audiences tend to stay away. 7 'Gods of Egypt' (2016) Gerard Butler as Egyptian God Set holding a weapon in the film Gods of Egypt Image via Lionsgate One of the biggest issues with Gods of Egypt was apparent to anyone with eyes who took even a cursory glance at the movie's poster. The pasty-white complexion of the major stars who were headlining this fantasy epic indicated a tone-deafness in the filmmakers that, if not actively hostile, was at the very least indicative of how misguided the film was going to be. The casting turned out to ultimately be a non-issue, as the film crashed at the box office thanks to bad word of mouth and reviews that took aim at its nonsensical plotting and overuse of unconvincing CGI . The movie was neither campy enough to enjoy as pure kitsch nor impressively sweeping enough to admire on a technical level. On its face, an epic action-adventure film steeped in the rich mythology of ancient Egyptian gods has a premise with a tomb's worth of potential, but Gods of Egypt's approach to its subject is so muddled that it renders it dramatically inert . The inaccuracies and liberties taken with the mythology are enough to turn away anyone with a genuine interest in it, and the comic-book approach to the characters is so plot-heavy and lore-dense that anyone who doesn't will quickly become confused or disinterested. Ultimately, it's just another failed fantasy epic that's mostly been forgotten alongside similar movies from the 2010s like Wrath of the Titans and Hercules . 6 'Megalopolis' (2024) A long-time passion project for Francis Ford Coppola , Megalopolis spent decades in development and was long-awaited by a certain group of cinephiles who were hoping it would be a triumphant return to form for the once lauded director of The Godfather and Apocalypse Now . Coppola financed the film himself and even paid for its advertising when the risk-averse studios refused. Everything about the film's production seemed to suggest the maverick filmmaker was producing something truly original and audacious that was bucking the dull trends of Hollywood epics. Unfortunately, the film turned out to be an overindulgent mess with laughably bad visual effects and a plot that has more ideas than it knows what to do with. The film's release was also plagued with reports of a chaotic production and allegations of inappropriate behavior by Coppola . Set in the futuristic city of New Rome, the plot, which was inspired by Roman history, follows Adam Driver 's rising architect Cesar as he clashes with the ruling class in his efforts to build the titular utopia. That's just the tip of the iceberg for a film that has a dozen disparate threads to it, some of which tie into its themes of America as a modern-day Roman Empire and others that swiftly disappear. It's certainly an unfiltered window into Coppola's mindset as a director, and it already has its defenders. It's the kind of excessive and indulgent film that almost always gains a cult following, but there's no arguing tha t Megalopolis is far from the masterpiece that many hoped it would be . 5 'The Great Wall' (2016) Matt Damon in 'The Great Wall' Image via Universal Pictures Few audiences or critics knew what to make of The Great Wall when its first trailer premiered. It was a strange historical epic involving supernatural monsters attacking the Great Wall of China, starring pony-tailed Matt Damon as a seemingly white savior hero. So much of it looked like a B-grade monster movie, which made A-lister Damon's presence in it baffling. Even more baffling was the fact that the film came from a highly regarded Chinese director, Zhang Yimou . Upon release, it turned out to be just as bizarre as every thought it would be. It was savaged by most critics and was a disappointment at the box office, and is now regarded as mostly a curio in the careers of its star and director . Set in 11th-century China, the movie follows two European mercenaries, played by Damon and Pedro Pascal , who are captured by Chinese forces and become embroiled in their battle with alien creatures. The movie was designed to be a crowd-pleasing blockbuster infused with Chinese culture that could be enjoyed by international audiences, but while Zhang still shows his talent for staging visually spectacular action, as he did in the far superior martial arts epics Hero and House of Flying Daggers , he's more ill at ease with the creature feature aspects and building the story around Damon's uninteresting protagonist. The Great Wall is stuck in a weird, dramatic middle ground where it never fully embraces its B-movie monster roots or successfully elevates them . 4 'Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker' (2019) Finn, Chewbacca, Rey, C-3PO and Poe all look onward on a sandy planet in Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker . Image via Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures If there's one thing the wet fart of a climax Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker did that should be commended, it's that it briefly united the otherwise deeply divided Star Wars fandom in their shared hatred of it. After the downright toxic and deeply unwarranted reaction to The Last Jedi sent the producers of the Disney sequels into damage control, they turned back to J. J. Abrams in the hopes that he would close out the trilogy in a way that would satisfy all the fans. Instead, Abrams made a movie that almost completely ignores the themes and ideas presented in its predecessor and tries to make a more direct companion to The Force Awakens that doubles down on nostalgia, continuity and common sense be damned . Offering unsatisfying conclusions to new characters Rey and Kylo Ren, while simultaneously sidelining others like Finn and Rose, the movie also brings back Ian McDiarmid as Emperor Palpatine, who has somehow returned from the dead, to act as the new big bad. As it turned out, there was no force powerful enough to get audiences to buy into the fan-fiction level writing as anything other than a bad Band-Aid over the open wounds the chaotic franchising by Disney had created. The Rise of Skywalker ended up being the most poorly reviewed of the live-action Star Wars films , which is an incredible feat in and of itself, considering how bad the prequels are for anyone who doesn't watch them with rose-tinted glasses . Indeed, The Rise of Skywalker is proof-positive that attempting to please all sides of a rabid fanbase will end up disappointing everyone. 3 'Rebel Moon' (2023) The cast of Rebel Moon standing aside one another in a wet alley Image via Netflix Maybe Star Wars fans should count themselves lucky that they got The Rise of Skywalker instead of Rebel Moon , which began as a pitch for a film set in the galaxy far, far away by co-writer and director Zack Snyder before it was rejected by Lucasfilm and picked up by Netflix. This big, bloated sci-fi epic — which was released in two parts, each with its own needlessly extended director's cuts with progressively dumber subtitles — is chock-a-block with cool visuals and slow-motion action. Narratively, though, it's so derivative that it inspires more apathy than genuine interest. It's yet another example of a film putting franchise ambitions first and story second , or in this case, probably third or fourth. Much like the similarly maligned, and Netflix-produced, Bright , this fantasy actioner was designed to be the beginning of a massive IP that could potentially continue in various sequels, prequels and spinoffs. World-building, however, makes for a much more interesting wiki article than a compelling film plot, and most audiences and critics were numb to the myriad subplots spread across the two-hour-plus runtime that were all pulled from better sources. Snyder, as a director, can undoubtedly deliver some compelling visuals, but they would be better served in a lean, mean 90-minute action movie instead of these kinds of would-be epics. 2 'Jurassic World: Dominion' (2022) Bryce Dallas Howard screaming in the face of a Dilophosaurus in Jurassic World Dominion. Image via Universal Pictures Like The Rise of Skywalker , Jurassic World: Dominion was a trilogy-capper that tried to pay homage to its entire franchise but fell completely flat thanks to bizarre story choices and an overabundance of nostalgia. The first Jurassic World was a serviceable return to the world of dinosaurs that overperformed thanks to audiences' desire to see more of their favorite prehistoric creatures on the big screen, and the sequel, Fallen Kingdom , was a Frankenstein monster of plotlines that had good direction but a bad screenplay. This final film seemed poised to give audiences the premise they had been continually teasing for years on end: Dinosaurs running amok in populated areas. While the movie does indeed feature some dinos in various cities and towns, the plot is far more focused on the new threat of deadly locusts and Chris Pratt and Bryce Dallas Howard globetrotting as second-rate spies. It also tries to bring back legacy characters played by Sam Neill , Laura Dern and Jeff Goldblum , but doesn't give them anything interesting to do. All of it feels like a soulless corporate product that's completely devoid of the awe and wonder that Steven Spielberg infused into the original film. Dominion still made over a billion dollars at the box office, but even Universal could tell that audiences were growing tired of the new characters and decided to reboot with the recently released Jurassic World: Rebirth . 1 'The Electric State' (2025) Millie Bobby Brown holding up a weapon and leading a group of robots and Chris Pratt in The Electric State Image via Netflix With Pratt having wrapped up his two big-budget franchises and Millie Bobbie Brown still in search of one that doesn't involve the Upside Down, the two stars teamed up with the Russo Brothers during their brief respite from the Marvel Cinematic Universe to make a film that proves flesh-and-blood creatives can still create something that feels like it was A.I.-generated. The Electric State is a sci-fi epic based on the illustrated novel of the same name, starring Brown as a young woman who sets out across a world ruined by war between man and robots to find her long-lost brother. Sadly, it contains precisely zero percent of its source material's haunting beauty or melancholy and instead is just a big, dumb actioner that has nothing interesting to say or any characters worth caring about. The Electric State should be the career nadir for Brown, Pratt and the Russos, who all collectively showed a ton of promise before getting swallowed up into franchises and otherwise mediocre vehicles, but based on the projects they all have lined up for the foreseeable future, audiences are more likely to be subjected to more of the same. The Electric State is the epitome of bad blockbuster filmmaking that has often plagued the current state of streaming-dominated cinema. Like any of its robot characters, it's shiny to look at, but it doesn't have any real heart or brains . Here are the best Terminator movies, ranked. What are the best Terminator movies as of 2025? The last Terminator movie was Dark Fate , released in 2019. And despite the franchise’s maybe most well-known line from the original, “I’ll be back,” we really don’t know whether the franchise will be making another movie anytime soon. That could be partly because of its box-office bomb, or we’ve moved on. Still, as far as movie franchises go, there’s always hope for the future. Just give it another decade (or less) and a different director. Terminator 2: Judgment Day (1991) We’re putting the sequel ahead of the original. This is one of those sequels that could be considered better than the original, right up there with The Godfather: Part II and The Dark Knight Rises . T2 took everything from the original and cranked up the volume. We have bigger action, better effects, but still get some actual heart out of the movie. Plus, Sarah Connor’s (Linda Hamilton, the legend) transformation into a full-on warrior and the T-800’s turn from villain to hero gave this one plenty to root for. It also still looks incredible decades later. Directed by James Cameron , Judgment Day takes us to 2029, when Earth has been torn apart by a war between Skynet and the human resistance. In a last-ditch move to secure victory, Skynet sends its biggest, baddest prototype Terminator back in time to kill resistance leader John Connor before he can grow up to lead the fight. Nip it in the bud, if you will. To protect John, the resistance sends its own reprogrammed T-800 back in time. Buy it on Amazon The Terminator (1984) In the original Terminator, James Cameron introduces us to a downright terrifying vision of the future. The year is 2029, and an AI defense network called Skynet has wiped out most of humanity. What survivors remain are trying to fight back under the leadership of John Connor. To stop him before he’s even born, Skynet sends a cybernetic assassin known as the Terminator (Arnold Schwarzenegger) back to 1984 Los Angeles to kill John’s mother, Sarah Connor. Despite being one of the most well-known sci-fi movies of all time, not everyone knows its wild origin story. James Cameron came up with the idea after a fever dream while working on Piranha II: The Spawning. He sold the script to producer Gale Anne Hurd for just one dollar, on the condition that he’d get to direct it himself. Because the film’s budget was so tight, much of it was shot guerrilla-style, meaning the crew often filmed without permits, rolling up to locations, shooting fast, and packing out before anyone could stop them. The Terminator went on to gross over $78 million worldwide on a $6.4 million budget. Buy it on Amazon Terminator 3: Rise of the Machines (2003) By the time Terminator 3: Rise of the Machines rolled around, it had been over a decade since Judgment Day. The future, as it turns out, wasn’t as changeable as Sarah Connor hoped. Directed by Jonathan Mostow (taking over for James Cameron), T3 catches up with John Connor as an adult, who is living off the grid. But Skynet isn’t one for submission, and sends an upgraded assassin known as the T-X. Once again, Arnold Schwarzenegger is back as the T-800, reprogrammed to protect John and prevent Judgment Day. Arnold Schwarzenegger was paid a mind-boggling $29.25 million for the role, plus 20% of the film’s profits, and $1.5 million in what’s called “perks”. He did have his work cut out for him at least, and insisted on doing many of his own stunts despite being in his mid-50s during filming. The movie went on to earn over $433 million worldwide, proving the franchise still had some steam. Buy it on Amazon Terminator Salvation (2009) Salvation is where things started to take a turn for the worse. Despite a stellar cast that included Christian Bale, Sam Worthington, Bryce Dallas Howard, and Anton Yelchin, the movie struggled to find its footing. Arnold Schwarzenegger was notably absent — he was busy being the Governor of California at the time — so the franchise’s biggest draw was missing right from the start. Set in 2018, Salvation finally takes audiences into the post-apocalyptic world the earlier movies hinted at. John Connor (Bale) is now a soldier in the human resistance, fighting Skynet’s army of machines. A mysterious half-man, half-root Marcus Wright (Worthington) shows up, and the lines between human and machine start to blur. On paper, Salvation should’ve worked: the war-torn wastelands, a darker tone, a fantastic cast, and no time travel. But somewhere along the way, it lost that spark that made the originals iconic. If we had to chalk it up to something, we’d say this one leaned too heavily on CGI and mechanical explosions (how very 2009 of it) but forgot humanity. Almost ironic, wouldn’t you think? Buy it on Amazon Terminator Genisys (2015) Arnold is back, and he’s got Emilia Clarke with him in this fifth installment, which did its best to reboot the franchise while ignoring all the previous sequels and the TV series. In this whacky timeline, Kyle Reese (Jai Courtney) is a soldier from the post-apocalyptic 2029. He’s sent back to 1984 to protect Sarah Connor, only to find out the timeline’s already been messed with — Sarah was raised by a reprogrammed Terminator she calls “Pops,” sent back to guard her as a kid. The movie hops across timelines and throws in a modern-day version of Skynet via an app called “Genisys,” which at least feels like a nod to today’s tech obsession. Some of the time-jumping actually works, and seeing Arnold back onscreen gives that classic feel-good nostalgia. Still, a lot of the movie ends up feeling like a mess of overlapping timelines and endless explosions. Buy it on Amazon Terminator: Dark Fate (2019) Dark Fate tries to hit the reset button, ignoring everything after T2 and bringing back the originals. Linda Hamilton returns as Sarah Connor! Arnold Schwarzenegger is back! We also get Mackenzie Davis joining the team as Grace, an enhanced human sent from the future to protect Dani Ramos (Natalia Reyes), the new target. Dark Fate’s setup is classic Terminator in prototype and runs the same gamut of humans versus unstoppable machines. The action is solid, the stunts are huge, and seeing Hamilton and Arnold back together is pure nostalgia gold. But despite all that, the movie cogs never quite clicked into place. And while this could be a personal opinion, the box office reflects that consensus. Maybe audiences had grown tired of reboots and timeline resets, or younger viewers didn’t have the same connection to the old-school characters. Still, it’s worth a watch to wrap up the full franchise marathon. Buy it on Amazon How we picked the best Terminator movies We picked the first five as the best for obvious reasons. The longer you go with sequels, the worse they tend to get — and the Terminator franchise is no exception. But since there are only six films in total, and we were going to pick five anyway, we just decided to rank them all and give you the full list. The Top 25 Horror Movies From The First 25 Years Of The 21st Century New Movies on Streaming: ‘Eleanor the Great,’ ‘The History of Sound’ + More The exact opposite of a spoiler alert: Jurassic World Rebirth ( now streaming on Peacock , in addition to VOD platforms like Amazon Prime Video ) features amok-running dinosaurs chasing and chomping on people. So it goes for the Jurassic Park/World franchise , which prompts one to ponder if these movies (or any number of other creature features, for that matter) would even exist if there wasn’t such a thing as the food chain. They also feature scenes prompting us to wonder why a carnivorous lizard the size of a modest skyscraper would even bother to doggedly pursue a single human for what amounts to one-eighth of a mid-afternoon snack – the effort is about on par with one of us walking several blocks uphill to consume a single gummy worm. It must simply be fun for the dinosaurs, I guess. But I digress. Jurassic World NO COLON Rebirth is the fourth in the World series, and a reinvigoration of the franchise. The slate is wiped clean for a fresh story, with all previous cast members (Laura Dern, Sam Neill, Jeff Goldbum, Bryce Dallas Howard, Chris Pratt, etc.) swapped out for Scarlett Johansson, Mahershala Ali and the inevitable small child who’s the equivalent of half of a metaphorical gummy worm, maybe less. Perhaps notable is how Rebirth has ONLY grossed $760 million compared to the $1 billion-plus of the previous three; it’s like, is making a few hundred mil instead of several hundred mil even worth the investment anymore? Perhaps those numbers are reflective of the obvious, that these movies do one thing over and over again to diminishing returns that are still obscenely profitable returns. Also obvious is that we kinda like that one thing. JURASSIC WORLD REBIRTH : STREAM IT OR SKIP IT? The Gist: Subtitle: SEVENTEEN YEARS AGO DOT DOT DOT. On the exotic island of Ile Saint-Hubert exists a crazy laboratory where scientists who are completely oblivious to the lessons of the previous Jurassic movies gene-splice the living crap out of dinosaurs to make mutant hybrids. Whoever came up with the idea for this needs to have their pancreas ripped out, beat with a pipe and reinstalled upside-down. Oh, there are reasons for this having to do with capitalism and drawing tourists to ogle nightmarish beasts, but the downside is, a simple candy bar wrapper with a prominent and recognizable logo (I will not mention the brand because it violates my personal ethics regarding egregious product placement in movies) can get stuck in a vent and cause the whole containment system to malfunction resulting in a yes-you-read-that-right mutant-ass D-REX to kill a man and prompt an evacuation. So it goes! PRESENT DAY DOT DOT DOT. It’s been 32 years since dinosaurs returned to Earth via humans doing DNA this and experiments that. As you may recall from one of the previous Jurassic World s, dinos are loose around the world and coexisting with humans. But the humans have moved on, bored with the general notion of giant lizards, which are dying off. I mean, a massive brachiosaur is ill and wandering through New York City, and all people can do is bitch about the traffic jam it caused, which leads me to believe that the true villain of this movie is one of the most gruesome and unstoppable beasts the world has known: ennuisaurus. It’s in the middle of that traffic tangle that “situational security and reaction” expert – read: mercenary who does dangerous and/or illegal stuff for massive pantloads of money – Zora Bennett (Johansson) is hired by Big Pharma guy Asshat Von Shitbird, er, I mean, Martin Krebs (Rupert Friend), to fetch dinosaur DNA for a landmark medicine that’ll cure heart disease. Granted, it’d take a serious brain disease to fetch the DNA, since it’ll have to be extracted from the biggest land, sea and air dinos while they’re still alive with their giant teeth and claws and territorial instincts and all those other dangerous things. Zora and Asshat Krebs need some help, though. Dr. Henry Loomis (Jonathan Bailey) is a paleontologist/NERRRRRRRRRDDD who can use the work now that his museum dinosaur exhibit is kaput due to lack of interest. He’ll venture with them, quite extralegally, into a forbidden zone near the Equator where the Mosasaurs, Quetzalcoatluses and Titanosauruses swim, fly and roam, respectively, combining to form the biggest Triple MacGuffin in cinema history. Zora, Krebs and Loomis will join forces with Duncan Kincaid (Ali) and his crew, and together they’ll all try to shoot a thingy into the aforementioned creatures that’ll automatically extract some blood then shoot itself back out and parachute down to our heroes. Simple! Then the mercenaries will go home with millions of dollars and the Asshat will invest the vials of goop into the capitalist machine to make trillions of dollars. Oh, and save some lives. Speaking of saving some lives. Elsewhere in the sea is a sailboat occupied by the McBaddecision family. There’s Dad McBaddecision (Manuel Garcia-Rulfo of The Lincoln Lawyer series ), Sis McBaddecision (Luna Blaise), Li’l Sis McBaddecision (Audrina Miranda) and Sis’ dopey boyfriend, Dude Comicrelieficzek (David Iacono). What are the chances that a Mosasaur will ruin their vacation by capsizing their boat, leaving them stranded in the middle of the ocean? Pretty good, actually, and that’s when their unnecessary more-than-a-subplot-but-less-than-a-regular-plot merges with Zora and Kincaid’s expedition, as the mercenaries rescue the helpless family and then get separated again after they’re stranded on Ile Saint-Hubert, only for the two parties to reunite deep in the third act, when everyone learns why humans no longer live in these here parts, and it has nothing at all to do with a lack snack-food brands with prominent and recognizable logos. No, it most likely has something to do with the mutant dinosaurs. Photo: ©Universal/Courtesy Everett Collection What Movies Will It Remind You Of?: I will use this space to propose crossovers with films Rebirth references and/or shares traits with: Jaws V: Mosasaur Mania , Godzilla x Kong x D-Rex and Dora and the Quest for Dino Doodoo . Performance Worth Watching: Although she does indulge a couple brief moments of introspection, ScarJo plays the least brooding-and-scowling movie merc ever. It’s as if she’s having fun and not taking any of this too seriously, which is precisely the point of the Jurassic World s. A little perk and pep goes a long way. Memorable Dialogue: A discussion of ethics: Loomis: What if we get the samples and don’t give them over to a company that makes a life-saving drug and then prices prices it so 99 percent of the plant can’t afford it? Science is for all of us, not just some of us. Have you thought about that? Zora: I guess I haven’t. Loomis: Well, maybe you should start. Zora: Maybe you should stop! Sex and Skin: None, and that’s a good thing, because the world is better off if none of these morons procreate. Photo; Universal Pictures Our Take: Jurassic World Rebirth is transporting and entertaining, but not transporting and entertaining enough to fend off my nagging curiosity about the dinosaurs’ motives. Basic hunger just doesn’t satisfactorily explain it. They don’t need another species’ corpses in order to gestate their young, like the Xenomorph in Alien . Are the dinos simply instinctual killing machines? Do they chase humans because they’re smaller and terrified and therefore good sport? Are humans a nutritionally dense superfood, like blueberries and salmon? The correct answer is obvious: The movies would be boring if dino no chomp chomp . That’s just Hollywood science, my friends. Then again, I recently watched Dangerous Creatures , which featured a zen moment between a woman and a great white shark roughly the size of a ’75 Cadillac Fleetwood, and that wasn’t boring at all, and in fact showed a daring amount of narrative innovation for a thriller with allegedly only cheep thrillz on its mind. That movie didn’t necessarily take the easy way out like Rebirth does, Edwards and writer David Koepp preferring to cruise by good, knotty ideas (e.g., a tossed-off line from Loomis about how human intelligence is no guarantee of survival, since we already have the means for self-annihilation) for conventional stuff like Corporations Are Bad and Helping People Is Good and Giant Lizards Hungy Nom Nom Nom. The pithy and brilliant assertion that Life Finds A Way went extinct several Jurassic movies ago. Then again, Dangerous Animals didn’t gross $760 million, so the makers of Rebirth know their audience prefers the eff-it-just-show-dino-carnage megabudget M.O. And I’d be a fool to argue that Edwards doesn’t spend $200 million well, executing that strategy with vigor and professionalism, especially visually, crafting a string of set pieces with spectacle spilling from all sides of the screen, thanks to a story that contrives encounters with the most gargantuan dinos existing in land, sea and air. And frankly, the director renders palatable a screenplay that feels like a sloppy rough draft, veering as it does between the more interesting Johansson-led mercenary plot and the bog-standard family-in-peril plot, where of course the little girl is situated adjacent to either giant sharp teeth or a cute little mini dino pal who’d make a great plushie. Some may take issue with Edwards’ shameless regurgitation of the teary-eyed moments of awe from the original Spielberg Jurassic Park , or the flatness of the omnipresent CGI. This is a franchise that tends to recycle its own fodder with the mercilessness of, I dunno, say, maybe a Big Pharma douche with dollar signs for eyes. But I looked past this irony with enough childlike wonder to have fun for a couple hours, and you will too. Our Call: I keep recommending these dumbass movies and feeling like a dumbass for doing it, but so be it. STREAM IT. John Serba is a freelance writer and film critic based in Grand Rapids, Michigan. Bohemian Rhapsody was the winner of four Oscars at that year’s ceremony. Fans adored it. Many people have told me it’s their favourite film of the past few years. I don’t get it. Granted, Rami Malek delivers a showstopping performance. But the film itself was a watered-down retelling of Freddie Mercury’s turbulent life - more concerned with playing it safe than telling his riveting story. Director Dexter Fletcher is who most people assume made Bohemian Rhapsody . In reality, Fletcher only came in for the final few weeks of production after Bryan Singer was fired. Fletcher was the man being thanked in the award speeches, despite it not really being his film. He needed his next project to be his own. Robin Hood was my lowest-rated film of that year. To understand why, just watch the opening ten minutes. It’s a disaster. Taron Egerton, the film’s lead, was starting to rack up a couple of duds. He needed his next role to remind the world how talented he actually is. Where does Rocketman tie into all of this? It’s the film that tells the world Dexter Fletcher is a director to be reckoned with, and that Taron Egerton is on his way to an Oscar. Rocketman tells the story of Elton John’s (Taron Egerton) rise to superstardom and the fall that followed. The story is cleverly told through flashbacks as Elton recounts his life at an AA meeting. Having Elton himself — an unreliable narrator - framing the story allows the film to break away from the traditional biopic mould. Instead of a straight retelling, Rocketman transforms into a musical fantasy. Key periods of his life are told through song. Numbers like The Bitch Is Back and Saturday Night’s Alright (For Fighting) are grand, over the top set-pieces filled with dozens of extras and a flurry of activity in the background. Each song pushes the story forward. It may sound like a family film. It isn’t. Elton is an addict, using drugs and sex to fill the void in his life. Unlike Bohemian Rhapsody , Rocketman doesn’t shy away from difficult subjects. Elton’s drug abuse is depicted in a way that never hides or glorifies his addiction. His sexuality isn’t hidden in the background either. Even though the press didn’t know about it at the time, the audience sees a man trying to embrace his true self in a world that won’t accept him. Rocketman takes risks, when judging by the previous year’s box office, it could have easily played it safe. Like Elton himself, this film is not interested in being normal. “Musical fantasy” wasn’t even a genre I knew existed before this. From start to finish, the film is magical, heart-breaking, intense and joyous. Elton John has both literal and metaphorical big boots to fill. He is one of the few artists alive who can be considered an outright superstar. Egerton not only does justice to the icon — he delivers a career-defining performance. Not once do you feel you’re watching an impersonation. This is a young actor proving he should never have been written off. From Elton’s plucky early years to the meltdowns of a directionless man, Egerton captures it all. It’s worth noting: Egerton does all the singing. No miming. He tackles songs that would terrify most vocalists. His dramatic chops, though, are what really make the performance soar. The final act, which dives into Elton’s downfall, is genuinely tough to watch. Egerton conveys the anxiety and heartbreak of a man everyone loves on stage but ignores off it. One scene, with him staring into a mirror, leaves you with goosebumps. It cannot be overstated: Egerton is extraordinary here. This is the performance of the year from a young actor who’d been teetering on a slump. By nailing this impossible role, he’s secured at least an Oscar nomination — and a career that will never again see him in something like Robin Hood . The supporting cast adds to the film magnificently. One of Rocketman ’s central themes is toxic relationships. The lack of love in Elton’s life fuelled his descent. Bryce Dallas Howard and Steven Mackintosh play Elton’s distant parents. Howard is unrecognisable as the overbearing mother with no interest in her son’s passions. I spent half the film trying to work out which English actress she was — I nearly choked on my popcorn when her name appeared in the credits. Mackintosh is superb as the father who refuses even to hug his child. Watching Elton’s upbringing is devastating, with only his grandmother (played with elegance by Gemma Jones) providing any warmth. Richard Madden is the real standout, playing Elton’s manager and former lover John Reid. Charismatic, intimidating, detestable - it’s a side of Madden we rarely see. Known for his noble roles, he relishes being cruel here, sparring with Egerton in biting exchanges. He feels like the Game of Thrones alumnus most destined for lasting stardom. Jamie Bell, meanwhile, plays Bernie Taupin - Elton’s only true friend and lyricist. Bell and Egerton share a delightful chemistry, portraying a lifelong friendship with real tenderness. Every supporting performance is grounded in character, never impersonation. Fletcher wasn’t making a tribute act - he was making a film. And what a film. Fletcher made all the right choices. The direction is flawless, with musical sequences that push boundaries. The Rocketman number itself is mind-bending. Fletcher gives the film the spirit of The Graduate , Chicago , and Almost Famous rolled into one. Crucially, he knows when to ease off the spectacle and when to let it rip. Having already worked with Egerton on the under-seen Eddie the Eagle , Fletcher clearly knows how to draw the best out of him. Lee Hall’s sharp script spares no one. Characters are never just good; they’re flawed, messy, real. Arguments carry the same weight as fight scenes. Cinematographer George Richmond paints vivid, lasting images that burn themselves into your memory. Together, Fletcher and his team have created something remarkable - a film that only a few years ago would have struggled to get made. Sensitive yet bold, honest yet fantastical, Rocketman is Fletcher’s declaration of intent. Whatever he makes next, the world will be watching. I had no expectations going into Rocketman . After Bohemian Rhapsody , I braced myself for disappointment. To say I was blown away would be an understatement. Sometimes a film just clicks into place - and this one does. The music, the direction, the acting, the heart: everything works. If you’re an Elton John fan, you’ll be delighted. If you’re a musical fan, you’ll be delighted. Even if you’re not into either, it doesn’t matter. Rocketman is the kind of experimental, risky film that isn’t supposed to succeed - but it does. If you’re a fan of cinema, you’ll love it. All rights reserved.', '33 Best Movie Trilogies of All Time: Fan-Voted Film Favourites Movies Reviews News Features TV Gaming Podcasts Empire VIP Empire Magazine Subscribe Manage My Subscription Newsletter Home | Movies | Features The 33 Greatest Movie Trilogies Of All Time – A Fan-Voted Countdown Decided By Thousands Cinema\'s best trios of films, as voted by you – the Empire readers by Ali Plumb , Helen O’Hara , and Phil de Semlyen | Updated on 16th November 2025 at 6.28pm In cinema, three has always been the magic number. From sweeping fantasy epics to gritty crime sagas the best movie trilogies represent storytelling at its most ambitious and satisfying. These aren\'t just three films released one after the other – they\'re carefully constructed narrative arcs that build worlds, explore core themes, and deliver emotional payoffs that single films simply can\'t match. The greatest film trilogies work because they understand the classic three-act storytelling structure: the introduction, the escalation, and the resolution. Whether it\'s watching a young farmboy become a Jedi Knight across a galaxy far, far away, following a teenager\'s adventures through time and space, or witnessing the rise and fall of a mafia family across generations, the best trilogy movies give us room to breathe, grow attached, and experience genuine transformation alongside their characters. From the action-packed thrills of globe-trotting archaeologists and time-travelling DeLoreans to intimate character studies from auteur filmmakers, movie trilogies span every genre and filmmaking approach imaginable. What makes certain trilogies endure while others fade? Sometimes it\'s the visionary director who maps out all three chapters from the start. Other times, it\'s the unexpected alchemy of a sequel that deepens what came before, transforming a standalone hit into something greater. And occasionally, it\'s the cultural moment they capture – the way the best trilogies of all time become iconic texts for entire generations, their quotes embedded in our conversations, their themes debated for decades. Like we said: it’s the magic number. How We Chose The Best Film Trilogies Compiling a definitive ranking of the best trilogies was never going to be a simple task. We started by asking you, Empire \'s passionate readers, to vote for your favourite all-time movie trilogies. Thousands of you responded, championing everything from pure three-film series untouched by prequels or sequels, to specific trios within longer franchises, to triptychs that were intended to be evaluated as a threesome even if they don’t share the same cast or characters. Where a coherent narrative across three films existed, we counted it – which is why you\'ll find certain trilogies here even when fourth or fifth instalments later emerged. Once your votes were in, we turned to Empire \'s experienced team of critics and contributors, asking them to weigh in with their expertise on the artistic merit, cultural impact, and lasting influence of each trilogy. We evaluated how well each trilogy functions as a complete narrative – does the third film stick the landing? Does the middle chapter avoid the sophomore slump? Do all three films come together to create something greater than the sum of their parts? After much heated discussion, countless rewatches, and vigorous debate about everything from superhero standouts to South Korean revenge thrillers, from comedy spoofs to zombie horrors , we arrived at our final ranking. Whether you\'re a devotee of groundbreaking sci-fi, animated classics or international arthouse cinema, you\'ll find something to love – and, probably, something to argue about – in our rundown of the greatest film trios ever made. So here, without further ado, is Empire \'s official ranking of the 33 (see what we did there?) best movie trilogies of all time... 33. The brand new season will see a return of some familiar faces as well as some new additions. View 2 Images Black Doves became a huge hit with fans when it was released back in 2024 (Image: Ludovic Robert/Netflix) Netflix teases: "Helen (Keira Knightley) is still betraying her nation’s secrets to the covert organisation she serves: the Black Doves. But after the misadventures of last Christmas , and with her husband Wallace (Andrew Buchan), preparing to become Prime Minister, she is walking a more treacherous line than ever. \u200c "As Helen’s enigmatic handler Mrs Reed (Sarah Lancashire) is ensnared in a ruthless plot to undermine her position in the Black Doves, Helen is reunited with her best friend Sam (Ben Whishaw). The once high-end triggerman is now reduced to lonely drinks in Soho bars and low-rate hits. "As they search for answers, loyalties are weaponised, trust is shattered, and the fight to protect the people they love could cost everything. With all the explosive wit of Series 1, Helen and Sam’s mission leads them back to old friends and enemies, through the dark decisions and painful sacrifices of their pasts, and right to the heart of the Black Doves." Keira Knightley, Ben Whishaw and Sarah Lancashire will return for Season 2 alongside Andrew Buchan, Kathryn Hunter, Ella Lily Hyland, Gabrielle Creevy, Agnes O’Casey and Molly Chesworth. \u200c View 2 Images Black Doves season 2 will see the return of some familiar faces as well as new additions (Image: Ludovic Robert/Netflix) New additions include Ambika Mod (One Day) playing Laila, an acerbic and anarchic Black Doves agent who is sent to help Helen on a mission as well as Babou Ceesay (Alien: Earth) plays Mr Conteh, a Black Doves executive with suspicious motivations. Sam Riley (Firebrand) plays Patrick, an emissary from a mysterious organisation, who offers Sam a lifeline, and fans may also recognise Neve Campbell (Scream) who joins the cast as Cecile Mason. \u200c Additional casting includes; Sylvia Hoeks (Blade Runner 2049) playing Katia Chernov, Goran Kostic (Canary Black and Ant-Man and The Wasp) playing Alexi Chernov and Samuel Barnett (Lee) playing Jerry. Writer and executive producer Joe Barton said: "I couldn’t be more excited to delve back into the world of our murderous little spy family. To have so many of our amazing cast returning and also being able to add some of my absolute favourite actors into the mix is such a great joy. Downing Street will never be the same again." As executive producers Jane Featherstone and Chris Fly teased season two will be "bigger, bolder and just as delightfully unpredictable". ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. That terror is at the heart of the former Austinite’s latest film, Vicious , which premiered at this year’s Fantastic Fest ahead of streaming on Paramount+. Bringing the film to the city that helped form him as a filmmaker and film lover was an undeniable thrill for Bertino. “The first time I saw a Cassavetes movie, the first time I saw a Terrence Malick movie, the first time I saw Polanski, all of these things happened in Austin. I saw the Texas premiere of The Big Lebowski here. The first time I worked on a movie, I was a PA on a grad student thesis at UT, and literally that day changed my life and I fell in love with movies.” The big question for any Gen X Austin film buff: Was he a Vulcan Video guy, or did he spend his time perusing the shelves at I Luv Video? “At one point I was Vulcan, and then I lived so close to an I Luv Video that I moved over.” It’s clearly the horror sections of both stores that influence his filmography, and Vicious is no exception. In it, Dakota Fanning plays Polly, a lonely and desperate woman who makes the mistake of opening her door to a mysterious visitor (Kathryn Hunter) carrying an even more mysterious box. It’s an immediately unnerving situation: After all, Bertino said, “There’s something inherently strange about an unexpected door knock, even in this day and age. A door knocks at nine o’clock at night and everybody turns and is like, ‘Who the fuck is that? What’s happening?’ Especially now, when everyone knows everybody’s step and everyone knows when everyone is coming. There’s something really cool about, in the middle of the night, a knock on the door that can change your life.” The question that emerges quickly for Polly is – why her? The terror comes from the possibility that there may be no reason at all. Bertino’s films have always been built around a certain horrifying ambiguity. In his breakout film, 2008’s The Strangers , the terror came from not knowing why the home invaders had decided to target that particular house. Similarly, with The Dark and the Wicked , the exact nature of the supernatural forces plaguing one family are unclear to the audience. However, Bertino himself is OK with that kind of uncertainty. “I’m a kid of the ’80s,” he said, “so parents didn’t talk to you, there was no therapy. I just went outside and threw a baseball against the wall and worked out my problems. But I honestly think that those kind of fears became a huge thing for me, with the realization as a boy that bad things happen and you don’t get the answer.” That sense of uncertainty seeped into his films, and into the films he watches. “I’m more frightened by what I don’t know than if I’m given all the answers. Because then I start to have a safety net and get to put it into an easier to control space. ‘Well, that will never happen to me because of X.’ No, bad things happen to all of us.” Moreover, he doesn’t think he’s alone as a storyteller in wanting to tell tales in these grey areas. “I think studios and financiers are scared of it,” he laughed. “I think there are more filmmakers interested in it than the movies themselves end up being. … I remember the first time I saw Scream in the movie theatre. I had seen Drew Barrymore’s face on the poster – ‘Oh, so she’s the star of the movie’ – and then I was shocked. Watching how that safety net got ripped away made everything a little scarier.” Writer/director Bryan Bertino on the set of Paramount Pictures’ Vicious Credit: Albert Camicioli; © 2025 PARAMOUNT PICTURES. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. However, just because the audience doesn’t necessarily know everything that’s happening, that doesn’t mean Bertino is equally in the dark. The question when it comes to the filmmaking is how much Bertino knows about the cosmology when he starts writing. Does he know exactly what’s happening, or is he feeling it out? “It’s a bit of both,” Bertino said, but with Vicious more than his other films it was much more about exploring the negative space. When he started writing, he explained, “I know what the box can’t do. … I automatically know, ‘I’m not going to let the box do this , I’m not going to let the evil have these powers,’ but I’m not always sure early on what it can do.” What clarified its limits for him was the process of exploring Fanning’s character. “The more I learned about Polly, the more I understood about the box because it was going to feed off of her.” Polly is quite literally the center of the film, and Bertino knew that his script was going to require a performer that could hold the audience’s attention and sympathies. “I’ve watched a lot of one-handers and they live and they die on not just the performance but the charisma. It’s like a singer on the stage that has a great album but then you see them live and they don’t carry that same thing.” While he was sure that Fanning was the kind of magnetic performer he needed, he was also playing with the audience’s familiarity with an actor who scored her first SAG nomination at the age of 7 for I Am Sam . In part, he was inspired by a quote from Alfred Hitchcock about Cary Grant, which he paraphrased as, “You cast certain people because the instant they walk through the door you’ve already done half your back story. … By casting Dakota, you immediately have all your childhood memories. You know what she looked like when she was 6, you know what she looked like when she was an awkward teenager, you have all those references, but at the same time she’s not that.” Fortunately for him, this was exactly the kind of challenge she was looking for. “She read a script in which there was blood and guts and crying and she was barefoot in the snow, and she was like, ‘Sign me up!’” Kathryn Hunter in Vicious Credit: Albert Camicioli; © 2025 PARAMOUNT PICTURES. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. When the ominous knock at the door comes for Polly, the fact that it’s a little old lady played by Hunter induces a state of confusion in the audience. Best known to American audiences for her performance as the witches in The Tragedy of Macbeth , her hilariously shocking turn as the sinister mother-in-law in The Front Room , and a small but memorable role on Disney+ show Andor , she was already a legend of the British stage and screen. Bertino said, “As I did research about her and came to realize all this work that she’s done in plays, and her amazing physical abilities and flexibility – she does yoga literally four times a day – but she has such a command of her voice.” Putting Fanning and Hunter together was pure magic for Bertino. “I’ve never seen that level of pure talent and control,” he said. “In much different ways, they had that same talent and that same ability. They know their bodies and every tool at their disposal, so it was really interesting watching them work together and find the scenes.” Vicious is streaming on Paramount+ now. By Jacob Robinson • @JRobinsonWoN November 18th, 2025 - 10:00 am Copy to clipboard Comments Picture left to right: Ambika Mod, Babou Cessay, Sam Riley, and Neve Campbell have been cast in Black Doves season 2. Netflix has finally confirmed that Black Doves season 2 filming is underway and rounded out the cast as it continues production in the United Kingdom, having begun in September. Ambika Mod, Babou Cessay, Sam Riley, Neve Campbell, Sylvia Hoeks, Goran Kostic, and Samuel Bennett have all been cast in Black Doves season 2. Here’s everything we know about the new cast members and their roles. One of the best new shows from 2024, Black Doves is a British crime-thriller series created by Joe Barton. It stars Keira Knightley as Helen Webb, a spy from a mysterious shadow organisation, who is publicly married to the British Defence Secretary. After the death of her lover, her secret identity as a spy is at risk, so the Black Doves send Sam, played by Ben Wishaw, to protect her. 7 New Cast Members for Black Doves Season 2 Picture: 7 new cast members for Black Doves season 2 Starting with Ambika Mod , she will play Laila, described as “an acerbic and anarchic Black Doves agent who is sent to help Helen on a mission.” The actress previously starred in the Netflix adaptation of One Day as Emma. Read Next Black Doves Season 2: Now In Production And Everything We Know So Far Babou Ceesay plays Mr. Conteh, one of the Black Doves executives with “suspicious motivations.” A new ally for Helen and Sam or a new antagonist? He recently starred in the Disney+ series Alien: Earth . Sam Riley will play the role of Patrick, “an emissary from a mysterious organisation, who offers Sam a lifeline.” Riley is best known for his roles as Diaval in Maleficent and Mr. Darcy in Pride and Prejudice and Zombies . Neve Campbell has joined the cast as Cecile Mason, who, interestingly, hasn’t been given any form of character description. Advisary or ally? We can’t wait to find out. Campbell is most well-known for starring as Sidney in the Scream franchise. Three further cast members have been revealed: Sylvia Hoeks (Blade Runner 2049) as Katie Chernov, Goran Kostic (Ant-Man and The Wasp) as Alexi Chernov, and Samuel Barnett (Penny Dreadful) as Jerry. Keira Knightley , Ben Whishaw , and Sarah Lancashire have already been confirmed to be reprising their roles as Helen Webb, Sam Young, and Reed. Picture: Ben Wishaw (left) and Keira Knightley (right in Black Doves Other confirmed cast members returning for season 2 are: Andrew Buchan as Wallace Webb, Kathryn Hunter as Lenny Lines, Ella Lily Hyland as Williams, Gabrielle Creevy as Eleanor, Agnes O’Casey as Dani, and Molly Chesworth as Marie. Production Underway on Black Doves Season 2 Alongside the casting news, Netflix confirmed that production on season 2 is underway, as it has been since late September 2025, with a planned wrap sometime in February 2026. Joe Barton, the series creator, had the following to say: “I couldn’t be more excited to delve back into the world of our murderous little spy family. To have so many of our amazing cast returning and also being able to add some of my absolute favourite actors into the mix is such a great joy. Downing Street will never be the same again…” The Vice President of Content for Netflix UK, Anne Mensah, shared her excitement Netflix has for the series return: “To say we are over excited about welcoming the Black Doves team back to Netflix would be an understatement. This is what happens when best in class writing meets best in class directing and extraordinary acting in a dark alley with guns and champagne. We couldn’t be more thrilled and we know the Black Doves fandom is waiting!” What is the Plot of Season 2? Netflix has provided an updated logline for Black Doves season 2: “Helen (Keira Knightley) is still betraying her nation’s secrets to the covert organisation she serves: the Black Doves. But after the misadventures of last Christmas, and with her husband Wallace (Andrew Buchan), preparing to become Prime Minister, she is walking a more treacherous line than ever. As Helen’s enigmatic handler Mrs Reed (Sarah Lancashire) is ensnared in a ruthless plot to undermine her position in the Black Doves, Helen is reunited with her best friend Sam (Ben Whishaw). The once high-end triggerman is now reduced to lonely drinks in Soho bars and low-rate hits. As they search for answers, loyalties are weaponised, trust is shattered, and the fight to protect the people they love could cost everything. With all the explosive wit of Series 1, Helen and Sam’s mission leads them back to old friends and enemies, through the dark decisions and painful sacrifices of their pasts, and right to the heart of the Black Doves.” For more information on the second season, you can find our ongoing preview here : Are you excited for Black Doves season 2 on Netflix? (Ludovic Robert/Netflix) Production has officially started on Black Doves season 2. Netflix has announced that cameras are rolling on the sophomore season of the spy thriller series starring Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw . The streaming service also revealed several new additions to the cast. One Day star Ambika Mod will play Laila, an anarchic Black Doves agent who has been sent to help Helen on a mission. Babou Ceesay is set to portray Mr. Conteh, a Black Doves executive with suspicious motivations, while Sam Riley will play Patrick, an emissary who offers Whishaw’s Sam a lifeline. Notably, Neve Campbell has also joined the cast, playing a character named Cecile Mason. Other additions include Sylvia Hoeks , who plays Katia Chernov, Goran Kostic , who takes on the role of Alexi Chernov, and Samuel Barnett , who plays Jerry. Sarah Lancashire , Andrew Buchan , Kathryn Hunter , Ella Lily Hyland , Gabrielle Creevy , Agnes O’Casey and Molly Chesworth all also return for season 2, which is now filming in London. Season 2 finds Helen (Knightley) still betraying her nation’s secrets to the Black Doves, according to its logline. “But after the misadventures of last Christmas, and with her husband Wallace (Buchan), preparing to become Prime Minister, she is walking a more treacherous line than ever,” the logline reads. “As Helen’s enigmatic handler Mrs. Reed (Lancashire) is ensnared in a ruthless plot to undermine her position in the Black Doves, Helen is reunited with her best friend Sam (Whishaw).” The show’s creator, writer and executive producer, Joe Barton , says he “couldn’t be more excited to delve back into the world of our murderous little spy family.” “To have so many of our amazing cast returning and also being able to add some of my absolute favourite actors into the mix is such a great joy.
